We synthesize a holistic taxonomy unifying hardware virtualization, cluster-level scheduling, and runtime inference optimizations, including iteration-level continuous batching, prefill-decoding disaggregation, and hierarchical KV cache offloading. Furthermore, we evaluate resilient cloud-native service architectures, examining scale-to-zero serverless paradigms, fault-tolerant checkpointing against silent data corruption, and hardware

papers.title: How AI Load Swings Reduce Datacenter Power Conversion Efficiency
papers.abstract: AI training and inference workloads make GPU power swing repeatedly between compute and communication phases. As a result, the cascaded converters in a datacenter rack keep moving between operating points with different efficiencies. This paper uses an energy based, cycle averaged method to quantify that effect along a 240 V AC to 400 V DC to 51 V DC rack power path, using measured efficiency curves of commercially available GaN based PFC and LLC converters. For a 1 Hz, 50% duty-cycle load swinging between 5 kW and 510 W, conversion efficiency falls to 95.97%, compared with 96.82% at the equivalent constant average load, a loss of 0.88%. When 51/48V to 1V point of load conversion to the chip rail is included, it is shown that the loss grows to 1.66% (89.45% vs. 90.96%). These results show that efficiency rated at average load overstates real world performance, and that the penalty grows with each load dependent conversion stage between the grid and the GPU.

papers.title: Embodied Emissions of 2.5D and 3D Scaling in Chipletized GPUs for Low-Carbon AI
papers.abstract: GPU compute resources are scaling to support growing AI workloads, leading to further rises in the climate change impact of hyperscale data centers that rely on high-performance GPUs. To model how packaging decisions impact the carbon footprint we have estimated the embodied emissions (EE) of a chiplet-based GPU that has been scaled in 2.5D and 3D using the imec.netzero modelling platform. We doubled the number of compute units and high bandwidth memory (HBM) capacity in the 2.5D and 3D scaled systems and found that 3D scaling results in an 89% increase in EE, as compared to an increase of 141% for 2.5D scaling, positioning 3D scaling as an attractive solution to limit the embodied emissions due to GPU scaling.

papers.title: Toward Open ISA Supercomputing: A Comparative Study of RISC-V, Arm, and x86 Architectures on HPC Workloads
papers.abstract: RISC-V is emerging as a candidate architecture for high-performance computing (HPC), but its competitiveness against established x86 and Arm processors remains difficult to assess because existing studies use different platforms, workloads, and methodologies, and rarely consider energy efficiency. Our work provides an evaluation of contemporary HPC RISC-V, Arm, and x86 processors using a common software stack and methodology. We characterize the Sophgo SG2044 and compare it with the NVIDIA Grace CPU Superchip and Intel Xeon Platinum 8480+ across four HPC benchmarks (STREAM, HPL, HPL-MxP, and HPCG) and four representative applications (iPIC3D, PLUTO, OpenFOAM, and llama$.$cpp). The version of HPL-MxP linked to OpenBLAS built and used for this work is made available as open-source software. The SG2044 reaches 8.02 GFLOP/s of FP64 performance and 7.8 GB/s of memory bandwidth per core, increasing to 294 GFLOP/s and 107 GB/s at 64 cores. L2-cache-aware process placement enables near-linear scaling up to 16 cores, beyond which memory-bandwidth saturation limits further gains. Across generations of RISC-V hardware, in the context of the Monte Cimone (MC) project, the SG2044-based MCv3 doubles both single-core performance and peak memory bandwidth relative to MCv2, while improving memory bandwidth, node-level FP64 performance, and energy efficiency by approximately 100x, 158x, and 10x, over MCv1. Against the Arm and x86 systems, the SG2044 shows 8-15x less absolute performance, refle

papers.title: Automated Multi-Line Bug Repair Using Model Checker Aided LLMs: A Case Study on RISC-V Processors
papers.abstract: Functional verification of Register-Transfer Level(RTL) designs has become a critical bottleneck in modern semiconductor development, often consuming the majority of project resources. Debugging, in particular, remains an especially time-consuming task, requiring careful analysis of simulation traces or counterexamples. Recent work has explored applying Large Language Models (LLMs) to RTL debug and repair with great promise. However, the existing approaches typically are for single-line bugs, operate in open-loop, rely heavily on prompts or retrieval, lack scalability, and often produce incorrect fixes. In this paper, we propose a novel automated RTL bug repair methodology that combines LLMs, assertions, and a model checker to provide scalable, trustworthy semantic grounding and formal guarantees. Concretely, the methodology leverages failing assertions to guide the LLM in generating patches for multi-line bugs. Each candidate patch is formally verified using a model checker (JasperGold), ensuring only valid repairs are accepted. We evaluate the efficacy and scalability of our methodology on the BRISC-V RISC-V core using mutation testing, introducing several mutation types, and demonstrate that our methodology can repair up to 98% of single-line RTL bugs and 93% of the multi-line bugs. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to show automated, LLM-assisted RTL multi-line bug repair results on a complex RISC-V processor design in a scalable manner.

papers.title: PARIS: Parallel Arithmetic Reduction and Integrated Selection for MSDF Inner Products
papers.abstract: Existing most-significant-digit-first (MSDF) accelerators serialize input-term processing, causing inner-product latency to increase with fan-in. This paper presents PARIS, an MSDF architecture that eliminates input-term serialization through parallel bit-plane reduction and shared carry-save residual selection. For $B$-bit operands, PARIS processes $B^2$ bit-position pairs, independent of fan-in within the supported tile, while generating exact MSDF outputs. Synthesized in 45\,nm at 100\,MHz, the 784-lane INT8 core occupies 0.008701\,mm$^2$ and completes an inner product in 88 cycles. Evaluation on two MNIST multilayer perceptrons demonstrates arithmetic-workload speedups of 240.44$\times$ and 180.47$\times$ over a matched reused-MSDF implementation, reducing arithmetic energy by 98.89\% and 98.58\%, respectively. A synthesized 16-engine accelerator occupies 0.90273\,mm$^2$ and meets the 100\,MHz timing constraint. Assuming immediate weight availability, it delivers a projected throughput of 24.33\,GOPS and an estimated energy efficiency of 1,581.14\,GOPS/W at unchanged mapped power. Bias-aware ReLU detection further reduces modeled arithmetic cycles by 5.52\% and 4.86\%. A separate 256-engine RTL implementation completes Model A in 259 cycles, demonstrating output-parallel scalability.

papers.title: TranSAGE: Automating Spatial Accelerator Generation for Large-Scale Transformer Models
papers.abstract: Large-scale Transformers have achieved remarkable success across NLP, computer vision, and robotics, but their growing computational and memory demands challenge efficient inference. Spatial accelerators offer advantages in on-chip bandwidth and energy efficiency, yet designing them for large models remains costly and time-consuming. Existing accelerator generators typically focus on single-operation support, overlooking the benefits of multi-operation pipelining, which limits throughput and energy efficiency. We propose TranSAGE, a compiler-based framework that jointly optimizes scheduling for large-scale Transformers under multi-operation pipelining and generates corresponding accelerator implementations. Our approach integrates a design space exploration (DSE) engine with multi-operation dataflow optimization and a dynamic programming-based graph partitioning algorithm to efficiently identify pipeline-friendly operation clusters and their optimal dataflow parameters. We further design spatial architecture primitives and lowering passes to automatically generate efficient RTL implementations. Evaluations on four representative LLMs demonstrate that TranSAGE achieves up to 2.41x higher throughput and 13.04x higher energy efficiency than commercial GPU/NPU baselines. Compared with state-of-the-art accelerator generators, TranSAGE achieves up to 11.33x higher throughput and 6.07x higher energy efficiency. Our code is available at https://github.com/sjtu-zhao-lab/TranSAGE.

papers.title: A Resource-Efficient and Precision-Scalable FPGA Accelerator for Spiking Neural Networks Using Minifloat Arithmetic
papers.abstract: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) are well suited to event-driven edge intelligence, but the arithmetic complexity, memory footprint, and power consumption associated with conventional floating-point implementations can limit their deployment on resource-constrained hardware. This paper presents a precision-scalable and resource-efficient SNN hardware accelerator architecture based on parameterized minifloat arithmetic. The proposed architecture implements recurrent leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neurons and leaky-integrator (LI) readout neurons using a unified minifloat datapath whose word length and mantissa width can be configured at synthesis time. A valid-driven arithmetic subsystem employs pipelined minifloat multiplication and addition, while time-multiplexed processing enables arithmetic resources to be shared across synaptic accumulation, neuron-state updates, recurrent connections, and output processing. This organization reduces replicated arithmetic hardware and provides a scalable design approach for different SNN sizes and precision requirements. The architecture supports E8M23, E5M10, E5M6, and E4M3 formats within the same RTL framework, allowing precision, memory capacity, timing, and power to be traded without modifying the underlying neuron architecture. FPGA implementation results demonstrate that reducing minifloat precision substantially decreases arithmetic-resource utilization and estimated dynamic power, while also reducing the theoretical storage require

papers.title: CCAaaS: An Orchestration Platform for High-Velocity Design, Development, and Deployment of Data Center Transports at Meta
papers.abstract: Today, data center networks run multiple congestion control algorithms (CCAs), each tailored to distinct traffic characteristics, from latency-sensitive intra-region RPCs to high-throughput cross-region AI workloads. The rapid evolution of AI training and inference further accelerates this trend by continually introducing new traffic characteristics that demand new CCAs. This paper introduces CCA-as-a-Service (CCAaaS), our eBPF-based ecosystem for the rapid design, deployment, and operation of production-grade CCAs at hyperscale. We present (1) a modular BPF-TCP framework and general lessons for designing modular CCAs; (2) a deployment and orchestration layer that provides disruption-free CCA updates, along with best practices for managing a zoo of CCAs at scale; and (3) a lightweight observability tool for CCAs and a blueprint for scaling CCA observability. CCAaaS manages over 97% of our server-to-server traffic using three active eBPF-based CCAs; two of the five CCAs we have built have since been deprecated. We show that our eBPF-centric approach to CCAs development delivers the same application-level performance (retransmissions, bandwidth, and tail latency) as their native in-kernel counterparts, and that our custom CCAs add negligible CPU and memory cost over their eBPF baselines. In terms of realized benefits, the CCA built with CCAaaS significantly improved network, and application metrics, for example, one of our CCAs reduced P99 latency for cross-region services by u

papers.title: SARIA: Persistence-Aware KV Caching with Coordinated DRAM--SSD Reload for LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Multi-turn LLM agents usually reuse long context prefixes, making key value (KV) caching crucial for reducing prefill latency. SSDs provide a low-cost extension to limited DRAM capacity but introduce two key challenges. Eagerly persisting all KV cache blocks incurs substantial write traffic and rapidly consumes finite SSD endurance. Meanwhile, the small number of SSDs provisioned in typical GPU servers limits aggregate reload bandwidth, making SSD-resident KV cache much slower to retrieve than that in DRAM and inflating prefill latency. We present \textsc{Saria} (Selective Admission and Reload for Inference Acceleration), a KV caching system that jointly manages DRAM and SSD by exploiting the session-level temporal locality of LLM agents to reduce SSD writes and accelerate cache reload. On the write path, \textsc{Saria} uses eviction and reuse history to selectively persist KV cache blocks that exhibit reuse opportunities beyond their DRAM residency, avoiding unnecessary writes for KV cache already hosted in DRAM. On the read path, \textsc{Saria} promotes selected SSD-hit KV cache blocks from GPU memory into DRAM after prefill, allowing subsequent reuse within the same session to reduce SSD read traffic while limiting DRAM contention. A transfer coordinator paces DRAM reads while SSD transfers are active, allowing both paths to make progress and efficiently share GPU ingress bandwidth. We implement \textsc{Saria} on LMCache MP and evaluate it using workloads from TraceLab and

papers.title: Aegis OS: A Transactional Multi-Tenant Operating System Runtime for Eliminating Authorization Fatigue in Autonomous Coding Agents
papers.abstract: Autonomous coding agents such as Google Antigravity (agy), Anthropic Claude Code (claude), and OpenAI Codex CLI (codex) execute multi-step software engineering workflows on workstations and cloud hosts. Existing agent environments face a Security-Autonomy Dilemma: operators must choose between per-action confirmation prompts, which interrupt workflows on 45%-57% of tool calls and induce authorization fatigue, or unconfined execution (--yolo / --dangerously-skip-permissions), which exposes host files, SSH/cloud credentials, and API tokens to prompt injection and hallucination risks. Furthermore, concurrent agents editing a shared working tree clobber one another's changes, while passing large artifacts inline through LLM context windows incurs high token overhead. We present Aegis OS (aegis-os), a transactional, multi-tenant Agent Operating System Runtime in Rust exposed via the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Google Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol. Aegis OS shifts the authorization boundary from individual tool calls to transactional workspace boundaries. Each agent runs inside a kernel-enforced OS sandbox (macOS Seatbelt and Linux Bubblewrap with default-deny --tmpfs $HOME isolation and a Unix-socket egress bridge) backed by a Copy-on-Write (CoW) shadow workspace (APFS clonefile; single-open Linux FICLONE reflinks), an identity-pinned HTTP Egress Proxy with L7 method/path-scoped secret injection and outbound DLP, and an A2A IPC bus with Content-Addressable Storage (CAS). papers.title: uGDS: A User-Space Development Kit for High-Performance GPU Direct Storage
papers.abstract: Data-intensive GPU applications increasingly rely on NVMe SSDs to extend GPU memory. NVIDIA GPU Direct Storage (GDS) enables direct SSD-GPU transfers via PCIe peer-to-peer DMA, eliminating host staging. However, GDS retains three key limitations: (1) its control path traverses the kernel for every I/O request, introducing software overhead; (2) its stream-ordered path imposes strict total ordering even when workloads only require batch-level ordering; and (3) its closed-source user-space engine hinders diagnosis and custom scheduling. We present uGDS, https://github.com/ScaleX-IO/uGDS, an open-source user-space GPU Direct Storage library built on four principles: user-space control, unified cross-vendor abstraction, workload-aware scheduling, and end-to-end transparency. The host CPU manages the entire NVMe command lifecycle in user space, while payloads move via PCIe P2P DMA without consuming GPU compute. A minimal kernel module is used only for one-time privileged setup. uGDS partitions hardware queues between synchronous and batch traffic, enforces DMA-safe buffer lifetimes, and provides cuFile-compatible synchronous, batched, and stream-ordered APIs with polling or interrupt completion on both NVIDIA CUDA and AMD HIP. Evaluated on an A100 with a Samsung 990 PRO, uGDS achieves up to 12.12x GDS's batch-read bandwidth and 30.69x its batch-write bandwidth (8- and 4-KiB requests, batch size 128), and reduces 4-KiB synchronous write latency by 84.1% with two threads. Its stream

papers.title: Breaking the Coupling: Efficient Concurrency Fuzzing for Linux Kernel Data Race Detection
papers.abstract: Detecting data races in the Linux kernel requires exploring both the input space and the thread-interleaving space. Existing kernel concurrency fuzzers couple these two searches by exploring interleavings during fuzzing, often spending substantial scheduling effort on inputs with little potential to trigger real races. In this paper, we present a new concurrency fuzzing paradigm that decouples concurrent-input generation from thread-interleaving exploration, enabling expensive scheduling to focus on promising inputs. To identify inputs that warrant targeted scheduling, we introduce May Race Pairs (MRPs), which represent conflicting memory-access pairs observed within a dynamically determined time threshold. Our framework first generates and executes concurrent syscall groups without controlled scheduling, collecting MRPs to guide further input mutation and identify schedule-worthy inputs. It then uses a separate scheduling instance to explore targeted interleavings and confirm real data races. To improve the effectiveness of both stages, we incorporate LLM-assisted semantic mutation for generating diverse syscall groups, backpressure-guided dynamic threshold control for balancing candidate production and scheduling consumption, and history-aware context recovery, context-aware interleaving scheduling, and candidate MRP prioritization for efficient race confirmation. We implement our framework for the Linux kernel and evaluate it on eight common kernel modules in Linux 6.17. I

papers.title: Decode Late, Multiply Once: Rethinking the Dot Product for Quantized Weights
papers.abstract: Large neural networks are increasingly deployed with 1-4 bit weights and 16- or 32-bit activations, yet their dot products still use one multiplier per element. We show that a length-n dot product with k-bit weight codes can be computed with n+2^k additions and at most 2^k decodes and 2^k multiplications. Each weight code is used directly as an address offset that selects one of 2^k accumulators; each activation is added into the selected accumulator; and the accumulated sums are decoded and multiplied only once, at the end, in a fused decode-and-multiply step. The decoded weight vector is never formed. The refactoring is exact for integer arithmetic, works with integer or floating-point operands and with arbitrary, including nonlinear, decoders, and extends to group-wise scales and to matrix and tensor products. The multiplier count falls by n/2^k, while total arithmetic energy improves by a smaller, bounded factor that we quantify with a cost model. We describe a scatter-accumulate processing element (SA-PE) that replaces the MAC unit in a weight-stationary systolic array, with a load/stream/reduce/drain schedule in which a small, time-shareable multiplier runs only 2^k times per tile. Because decoded weights are not stored, local weight memory shrinks by up to w_d/k for w_d-bit decoded weights. An RTL implementation synthesized for FPGA and compared with a matched MAC array shows that an unshared SA-PE is larger than a MAC PE, and that the saving appears when the reduction

papers.title: Fast Path, Exact Path: One Library of Hardwired Operators for Streaming and Exact Canny Edge Detection on a Low-Cost FPGA
papers.abstract: Hysteresis edge tracking, the final stage of Canny edge detection, follows edge chains of unbounded length and therefore resists single-pass streaming; FPGA designs either approximate it or dedicate separate labelling hardware to it. We show that a single library of hardwired 3x3 operators, each with an identical two-clock latency, delivers both a camera-rate approximation and exact hysteresis on a low-cost Artix-7 (XC7A35T). The fast path streams camera pixels through the operators and K local hysteresis stages and commits each edge decision 262.15-720.63 microseconds after the pixel arrives (K = 1-8; system simulation with a datasheet camera model), that is, 3 + K camera lines later and 46-127x sooner than a frame-based processor can even begin at 30 frames per second. It provably never reports an edge that exact hysteresis rejects, recovers 76.6-96.1% of exact edges at thresholds 20/40, and on the 200 BSDS500 test images retains at least 98.6% of the exact path's boundary F-measure (ODS 0.470-0.477 versus 0.476). The exact path holds 128x128 tiles in block RAM, is exact within each tile, and replaces two-buffer iteration with in-place forward and reverse sweeps built into the same operator. This reduces hysteresis from 38-82 passes to 3-7 on pattern and photo tiles, accelerating the hysteresis step 6.6-21.7x (40x on a worst-case tile) and a complete tile 4.5-9.9x, with identical output. Both paths are bit-exact with software golden models at every pipeline stage and close

papers.title: Ray-by-Ray: Fine-Grained Resource Management for GPU Ray Tracing Units
papers.abstract: Ray tracing (RT) generates photorealistic images by simulating the physical behavior of light as it interacts with surfaces in a virtual scene. In film production and high-end rendering pipelines, this technique computes global illumination, reflections, refractions, and soft shadows by tracing millions of light rays per frame and accurately modeling their bounces and attenuation. Contemporary GPUs incorporate specialized ray tracing hardware to accelerate key operations in the traversal pipeline. By accelerating these stages in hardware, the unit enables real-time ray tracing for complex scenes that previously required offline computation. However, ray tracing introduces substantial control and data divergence. Each ray may traverse a different set of nodes in the acceleration structure, encounter distinct materials, or terminate at varying depths. This irregularity reduces thread coherence and exposes a fundamental disparity between the GPU SIMT and per-thread execution model of dedicated RT units, where each ray progresses independently. In this work, we seek to validate assumptions made in open-source infrastructure and identify potential inefficiencies in resource management within the ray tracing pipeline. To address inefficiency caused by mismatches between SIMT and RT granularities, we propose Ray-by-Ray, which decomposes on-chip buffers into the granularity of individual rays and introduces lightweight management structures that enable more warps to run in parallel w

papers.title: EGGPlacer: Energy-Guided Generative Chip Placement with Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: Chip placement strongly affects routed wirelength and thermal behavior, yet these downstream metrics are difficult to evaluate during macro placement. Learning-based macro placers commonly optimize the macro-only half-perimeter wirelength (HPWL), denoted mHPWL, which ignores standard cell connectivity and spatial demand. In contrast, analytical mixed-size placers optimize differentiable full netlist wirelength and density objectives but are typically unaware of thermal effects. We propose EGGPlacer, an energy-guided diffusion framework that incorporates analytical placement feedback and thermal feedback into macro placement generation. An analytical placer acts as an online physical response model, exposing the standard cell distribution and a full netlist wirelength proxy induced by each intermediate macro placement, while a differentiable thermal model provides temperature feedback. These signals are formulated as composable energies and injected throughout reverse diffusion without retraining the underlying generative model. Experiments on public placement benchmarks show that EGGPlacer achieves competitive mixed-size HPWL relative to strong analytical and learning-based macro placers. In the end-to-end evaluation, EGGPlacer also obtains the lowest average routed wirelength and peak temperature among the evaluated methods. Ablation studies further demonstrate that analytical and thermal guidance provide distinct and complementary benefits across wirelength proxies, routed

papers.title: SnakeCharmer: Orchestrating Utility, Timeliness, and Placement in GPU Prefetching
papers.abstract: GPUs rely on massive thread-level parallelism to tolerate long memory latency, yet they still suffer severe stalls when many warps simultaneously wait for data from the memory system. Address-prediction-based GPU prefetchers can mitigate such stalls, but accurate prediction alone does not guarantee performance improvement: a predicted prefetch becomes beneficial only if it is worth issuing, arrives at the right time, and is retained without harmful interference. Because these requirements interact, optimizing any single dimension in isolation can simply move the bottleneck to another. We capture these requirements with a predicted-prefetch-to-realized-benefit perspective and propose SnakeCharmer, a unified backend prefetch-control framework for address-prediction-based GPU prefetchers. SnakeCharmer separates address prediction from prefetch realization: the frontend predictor generates prefetch candidates, while the backend control path jointly controls utility, timeliness, and placement by determining whether each candidate should be issued, when it should be issued, and where the returned data should be retained. SnakeCharmer realizes this control path with zero-value-aware filtering for utility, hierarchical feedback-driven distance tuning for timeliness, and a register-assisted prefetch buffer for placement. We design and implement SnakeCharmer primarily on top of Snake, and adapt the same backend-control principles to APOGEE to demonstrate that SnakeCharmer's benefits ar

papers.title: RV565: Cross-Layer Co-Design for Frame-Independent Video Playback on MicroPython-Class ESP32-S3 Systems
papers.abstract: Video on SPI-attached microcontroller displays is limited less by decoding than by where each byte lives and which stages run serially. We present RV565, a decode framework for frame-independent video whose decoded representation is the panel's native RGB565 format, and evaluate it on an ESP32-S3 with two ten-second windows of an openly licensed film. A serial path - inflate, then scale into internal-memory stripes overlapped with SPI direct-memory-access (DMA) transfers - meets the 41.7 ms deadline on the lighter window but misses all 7,200 frames of the heavier one. RV565's dual-core pipeline inflates the next frame on the second core during the transfer and sustains 24 FPS with zero misses and 10.3 ms of slack on both windows; frame time then equals the display transfer, which runs at 98.1% of the 40 MHz wire-time bound. Because frames are independent, inflation time is linear in the compressed length stored in the container (pooled r^2 = 0.9987): a model fitted on one window predicts the other within 0.04 ms and identifies from metadata alone which window the serial path cannot schedule. We show why Deflate cannot exploit co-located temporal redundancy in RGB565 frames larger than 128x128 pixels and measure the price: a shared Deflate stream changes size by at most 1.1%, whereas an explicit XOR delta would save 46-80%. Inside OreoOS, a MicroPython application operating system, firmware inflation alone reaches 12.2 FPS; stage timing attributes the 80.4 ms frame time to ser

papers.title: HDLouvain: High-Throughput Incremental Clustering for Hyperdimensional Data
papers.abstract: Modern shotgun proteomics generates tens of thousands of tandem mass spectra per hour, producing hundreds of gigabytes of data that strain conventional clustering pipelines. DBSCAN and hierarchical agglomerative clustering (HAC) offer flexible similarity search, but DBSCAN is unstable across varying data densities, HAC costs $O(n^2)$, and both yield poor cluster quality. Graph-based methods such as Louvain produce high-quality clusters but scale poorly on streaming data. We observe that Louvain's poor scalability can be resolved without sacrificing its quality, and present HDLouvain, which combines Louvain community detection with the bit-parallel similarity computation of hyperdimensional computing (HDC). HDLouvain partitions a bootstrap fraction of the stream into precursor-mass buckets, applies Louvain to each bucket's kNN similarity graph, and condenses each community into a single binary hypervector by bitwise-majority bundling rather than iterative centroid recomputation. New spectra are assigned by a GPU-accelerated Hamming distance lookup against representatives in their mass bucket, or seed a new cluster when no match meets a similarity threshold $τ$, so the partition grows incrementally without full re-clustering. On five PRIDE datasets (0.99M to 21.13M spectra), sweeping the bootstrap fraction $α$ from 0.2 to 0.9 exposes an explicit, monotonic throughput-fidelity trade-off. On PXD003258, speedup ranges from 4.5x at $α=0.3$ to 1.65x at $α=0.7$. Modularity rises from

papers.title: Typed Template Fuzzing
papers.abstract: Fuzzing software with complex inputs has been a longstanding challenge. Traditionally, fuzzers either programmatically encode language constraints, requiring significant engineering effort, or rely on users to declare grammars and constraints. Recent LLM-based fuzzers address these drawbacks but introduce new issues. Some use LLMs for test generation, sacrificing throughput and producing invalid inputs when the LLM makes mistakes. Others rely on language-specific parsers, static analysis, and AST manipulation libraries. We introduce Typed Template Fuzzing (TTF), a lightweight LLM-based fuzzing methodology. The key idea is to use LLMs in a preprocessing step to transform seeds into typed templates. The typed templates then enable semantically aware, mutation-based fuzzing without language-specific parsers, type checkers, or further LLM queries during fuzzing. By exploiting the correspondence between seeds and templates, TTF can moreover repair LLM mistakes. We have implemented TTF in our tool Typos, which we evaluate across 21 input languages, including C, C++, Go, Rust, SystemVerilog, Scala, and Java, as well as libraries such as PyTorch and Qiskit. In a six-month fuzzing campaign, we reported 135 bugs, 128 of which were previously unknown. Perhaps most notably, on average 96% of Typos's mutants are valid, coming close to the validity rates of domain-specific fuzzers. Our evaluation further shows Typos's benefits over the state of the art.

papers.title: FIGFLEX: A Mixed-Precision FP-INT GEMM Accelerator Co-Designed with Low-Bit LLM Quantization
papers.abstract: Weight-only quantization keeps LLM activations in floating point and stores weights as low-bit integers, turning the dominant workload into floating-point-integer (FP-INT) general matrix multiplication. Recent quantizers reach a 2-3-bit average with mixed precision, but hardware has not kept pace: GPUs dequantize weights to FP16 before the tensor-core multiply-accumulate, and bit-parallel FP-INT accelerators run at a single weight precision, so fewer bits save memory but not computation. In this paper, we present FIGFLEX, an algorithm-hardware co-designed mixed-precision accelerator whose bit-parallel datapath scales throughput as precision falls. FIGFLEX contributes (1) a shift-add, radix-4 reformulation of FP-INT multiplication that fuses the multiply-accumulate into a unified, precision-flexible partial-product reduction and roughly halves the partial products, together with a novel INT3 optimization that reclaims the idle datapath radix-4 leaves at that precision; and (2) a mixed-precision quantizer that assigns each channel group its bit-width according to the error GPTQ cannot compensate, with a per-input-channel column scaling whose power-of-two normalization keeps the scaled activations out of the FP16 subnormal range, so that the quantized model maps directly onto FIGFLEX's datapath with the same accuracy as on a GPU. On LLaMA-2-7B, FIGFLEX attains 5.85 and 8.77 WikiText-2 perplexity at 3- and 2-bit average precision, lower than GPTQ, AWQ, SliM-LLM, AMQ, and QuIP# (w

papers.title: Proba: A High-Performance, Low-Traffic Probabilistic Spatial Memory Streaming Prefetcher
papers.abstract: Spatial Memory Streaming (SMS) prefetchers exploit recurring spatial access patterns across memory regions to predict future accesses. Despite their effectiveness, existing SMS-based designs suffer from coarse control over aggressiveness and limited adaptability to dynamic program behavior and historical patterns. In this work, we present Proba, a feedback-directed SMS-based prefetcher that integrates probabilistic pattern updates, marginal accuracy decision-making, and pattern accumulation over several trigger features to achieve fine-grained accuracy-coverage trade-offs. When accuracy deteriorates, Proba moderates its aggressiveness to prioritize accurate prefetches; conversely, when accuracy rises, it expands its coverage. Proba achieves higher speedups than any other SMS-based prefetcher while being vastly more efficient in DRAM traffic. This culminates in a large performance gap between Proba and other techniques in multicore and DRAM-constrained scenarios without harming single-threaded throughput.

papers.title: AnalogPortBench: Benchmarking LLMs on Analog Circuit Porting
papers.abstract: Analog circuit design still relies heavily on expert knowledge, and porting proven designs to new process nodes is a recurring bottleneck. As a lower supply reduces available voltage headroom, a working topology may require redesign or fail to meet specifications. While large language models (LLMs) have begun to generate and optimize analog circuits, existing benchmarks focus on one process node and assume feasible specifications. To bridge this gap, we introduce AnalogPortBench, a benchmark of 54 tasks for porting ten circuits, from current mirrors to telescopic amplifiers, from a 0.18 $μ$m process to the open-source SKY130 PDK. Tasks range from a direct port through a reduced supply and harder specifications to infeasible ones, and every feasible task has a reference design verified at five process corners. Evaluating six frontier LLMs at two reasoning levels, with and without simulation feedback, we find that models port simple circuits but rarely re-design headroom-sensitive amplifiers, seldom recognize infeasible specifications, and gain more from simulation feedback than from more samples or reasoning. Code and data are available at https://github.com/saeidrajabii/AnalogPortBench.

papers.title: Verified DRAM Address Mapping Reverse Engineering with Threshold Sweep
papers.abstract: We propose an end-to-end software pipeline for solving and validating DRAM address mapping functions on embedded LPDDR5 systems, and we instantiate it on embedded platforms. Starting from a large latency dataset of address pairs, the pipeline first builds a latency histogram and then performs a threshold sweep to obtain candidate same-bank address pairs. For each threshold, we apply a Knock-Knock-style linear-constraint solver to recover candidate bank masks. Final bank masks are calculated using GF(2) reduced row echelon form (RREF). To verify correctness, we implement two verification stages, group verification and single function verification, inspired by prior work. Group verification checks whether bank partitions induced by the recovered masks agree with observed timing behavior. Single function verification removes one addressing function at a time and measures the resulting change in verification pass rate. Unlike approaches that return only a single inferred mapping, our workflow systematically records, for each candidate threshold, the solved bank masks and validation metrics. This pipeline supports more robust selection of bank masks on ARM-based embedded devices and provides an efficient method for reverse engineering DRAM address mapping functions and subsequent Rowhammer analysis.

papers.title: HAWK: Heterogeneity-Aware KV Cache Transfer for Efficient GPU-NPU Phase-Disaggregated LLM Inference
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference exhibits distinct computational characteristics across its two phases: prefill is compute-intensive, whereas decode is more memory-bound. As a result, AI accelerators achieve varying levels of efficiency across the two phases. GPUs are well suited to prefill, but are often underutilized during decode. By contrast, NPUs can utilize their compute resources more effectively during decode. Motivated by this observation, we explore a heterogeneous architecture that integrates GPUs and NPUs, mapping prefill to GPUs and decode to NPUs to achieve high performance and efficiency. However, realizing such heterogeneous integration is challenging because LLM phase disaggregation requires KV cache transfer from prefill to decode (that is, from GPUs to NPUs), which is complicated by differences in inter-device communication mechanisms and KV cache tensor layouts. To address this, we propose HAWK, a transfer mechanism that enables rapid KV cache transfer across heterogeneous devices. HAWK establishes a remote direct memory access (RDMA) path for direct cross-device transfers while handling inter-device tensor layout discrepancies as part of the transfer process. In particular, HAWK allocates tensor-layout-aware RDMA buffers on the NPU side to match the target tensor layout. Leveraging these buffers, HAWK orchestrates data transfer from a conventional contiguous GPU RDMA buffer to the corresponding NPU buffers, allowing transferred tensors to be consumed

papers.title: TernScope: Model-Hardware Co-Design for Efficient Ternary Endoscopic Segmentation
papers.abstract: Edge medical segmentation must reconcile small model size, high accuracy, and fast inference. TernScope addresses this tradeoff through model--hardware co-design, learning a compact segmentation network whose low-bit operators also simplify hardware execution. Split-channel large-kernel blocks preserve spatial context with limited computation, while branch fusion removes redundant inference paths. Ternary Progressive Quantization-aware Training (TPQ) then adapts the fused network from deep to shallow layers, through the decoder, and finally to the input and prediction layers. All 25 convolutions use ternary weights and 8-bit activations, enabling packed storage and multiplier-free computation. The resulting model uses 0.2483 M parameters and 0.0949 GMACs while retaining competitive segmentation accuracy on in-domain and external datasets. Under the same 45 nm technology, TernScope reduces compute-array area by 88.46% compared with the original Gemmini, a systolic-array accelerator with 8-bit $\times$ 8-bit multipliers. These results demonstrate a path from accurate lightweight medical segmentation to compact low-bit hardware.

papers.title: Hard and Soft Real-Time DNN Inference Scheduling on Heterogeneous Multi-Accelerator Systems via Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: We present a scheduling framework for heterogeneous multi-accelerator systems executing both hard real-time and soft real-time QoS-aware DNN inference workloads. The framework combines an online reinforcement learning (RL) scheduler with a deterministic runtime safety layer. The RL scheduler dynamically generates candidate schedules by jointly selecting sub-job priorities and accelerator assignments, while runtime certification guarantees that all HRT deadlines remain satisfied independently of the learned policy. To enable runtime certification in heterogeneous precedence-constrained systems, we introduce a schedulability-preserving prefix replacement criterion based on machine-wise cuts. The proposed criterion guarantees that runtime-generated schedule prefixes preserve the existence of a feasible continuation without requiring complete finish-time dominance with respect to a feasible reference schedule. Experimental results on heterogeneous DNN accelerator platforms show that the proposed framework preserves HRT schedulability while improving QoS-aware deadline satisfaction, client-level service quality, and accelerator utilization compared to state-of-the-art scheduling approaches.

papers.title: Reorienting the Vector Axis: Restructuring FlashAttention for Long-Vector Processors
papers.abstract: A Transformer is built around attention, whose cost grows with the square of the sequence length and dominates the layer on long sequences. FlashAttention made that cost manageable by tiling the attention matrix and updating the softmax as it goes, but almost all work since has targeted GPUs. On long-vector processors one vector register can hold up to 512 single-precision numbers. The savings of a vector instruction are proportional to how much of the register it uses, so the choice of which loop to vectorize is a first-order decision. We port PyTorch's CPU FlashAttention kernel to a RISC-V CPU with 2KB vector registers and find that it reaches 16.2% of peak floating-point throughput. The kernel walks each tile one query row at a time: the product against V is vectorized along the 64-element head dimension, the softmax's per-row maximum and sum are reductions that collapse a full register to a scalar, and the software exponential's polynomial coefficients compete with tile data for vector registers and cause spilling. We propose two techniques. The first transposes the score tile and the running output so that queries lie along the contiguous axis. The algorithm and its values are unchanged. A single parameter, the number of queries in a tile, now sets the vector length of every part of the kernel and can be matched to the machine. Both reductions also disappear. The second moves the polynomial's coefficients into scalar registers, removing the spills and cutting the softmax

papers.title: Deciding Scale Placement in MXFP4 Dot Products with Integer Arithmetic
papers.abstract: The Open Compute Project's microscaling (MX) family includes MXFP4, which stores 32 four-bit elements with a shared power-of-two scale. When lowering a dot-product reduction, a compiler can apply these scales before the reduction, or defer scaling until afterwards. Although equivalent over real numbers, these formulations can produce different IEEE binary32 results through overflow or underflow, with equivalence also depending on the reduction tree. We study the legality of compiler rewrites in either direction by deriving conditions under which the two formulations are bitwise equivalent. To decide rewrite legality, we construct an integer state machine that exploits the finite element alphabet and shared power-of-two scales, modeling overflow, NaN, and subnormal rounding. We prove its faithfulness under bounded scale codes and integer coefficients, yielding an exact encoding of the equivalence query in quantifier-free linear integer arithmetic (QF_LIA). For MXFP4, we derive a closed-form sufficient upper bound on the sum of scale exponents for any fixed binary reduction tree within the supported coefficient range. This bound depends on the size of the largest proper subtree. For four tree shapes at block lengths $k\in\{2,3,4,8,16,32\}$ and two shapes at $k=64$, SMT finds counterexamples when this upper bound is increased by one exponent step. Against the standard direct encoding in quantifier-free floating-point arithmetic (QF_FP), on matched queries cvc5 proves the integer

papers.title: Double KV Cache Optimization on Apple Silicon: Block-FP4, Radial Quantization, and Fused Metal Kernels
papers.abstract: Key-value (KV) cache capacity and memory traffic are primary bottlenecks in long-context autoregressive inference. We evaluate five cache paths on an Apple Silicon M5 Max using MLX: a native bf16 baseline, block-scaled E2M1 FP4, a Python reference implementing radial quantization with a QJL-style residual, sequential FP4-to-Polar composition, and a fused Metal Polar kernel. On Apple Silicon M5 Max, fused Metal PolarQuant achieves 46.8 tok/s at 3,456 B/token - 3.64x compression versus the bf16 baseline and 1.84x faster than the Python Polar reference (25.4 tok/s), while slightly outperforming block-FP4 (41.5 tok/s at 3.62x compression). Sequential composition of FP4 and Polar (Double Optimization) yields no additive benefit: 4,241 B/token at 15.1 tok/s, worse than FP4 alone on both axes. The fused path establishes that radial coding can be competitive when packing, rotation, and reconstruction are placed in one device kernel, but this result does not extend to longer contexts. At 32K and above, all compressed variants collapse to 1.5-14 tok/s because the current attention path repeatedly reconstructs the full cache, retaining cumulative O(N^2) decode work. At 64K, the Metal variant runs out of memory when a 33.5 GB allocation exceeds MLX's 22.6 GB Metal buffer limit. Fused scaled dot-product attention operating directly on compressed KV, together with chunked pre-allocation, is required for long-context viability. These results separate representation-level compression from ke

papers.title: JANUS: Agentic Cross-Language Fuzzing Harness Generation for Android Native Libraries
papers.abstract: Modern Android apps extensively rely on native libraries, bridging Java/Kotlin and C/C++ through the Java Native Interface (JNI). This cross-language interoperation, however, exposes the memory-safe Android Runtime to the unsafe C/C++ world, creating an attack surface that has been repeatedly exploited for full device compromise. While fuzzing is a proven technique for vetting native libraries, state-of-the-art harness generation tools struggle to faithfully capture closed-source cross-language API usage: (i) precise program analysis across the JNI boundary does not scale, whereas lightweight approximations miss critical invocation patterns; and (ii) none tackles the construction of complex composite objects consumed by JNI methods. In this paper, we propose JANUS, the first agentic approach to synthesizing cross-language JNI-aware fuzzing harnesses for Android native libraries. JANUS iteratively resolves both explicit and implicit cross-language call dependencies to recover app-specific runtime context, and recursively assembles cross-language argument objects in a bottom-up manner. JANUS leverages an autonomous agentic workflow to reduce reliance on hand-crafted heuristics, capturing the vast landscape of hidden API usage knowledge embedded in closed-source native libraries. Evaluation on 44 popular real-world apps (such as Google and YouTube Music, covering 21,386 JNI methods total) shows that JANUS produces over 5.9 times as many valid harnesses (6,094) as state-of-the-ar

papers.title: Do Coding Agents Understand Why Systems Crash---and Why They Don't?
papers.abstract: Coding agents are increasingly capable of fixing real-world bugs, yet they still struggle with large systems codebases such as the Linux kernel. To understand why, we test how agents reason about execution in these codebases through crash reasoning: predicting from source code whether a given input crashes the system. A correct prediction alone, however, does not establish this ability, since it may come from merely spotting suspicious code. In this paper, we propose source interventions: we pair source trees that differ by a single commit, so that the same input crashes only one of them, and test whether agents predict crashes more often on the crashing tree. Experiments with four coding agents on SysRB, our dataset of 934 such pairs from Linux and OSS-Fuzz projects, yield three main findings. First, agents are biased toward predicting no crash: they rarely raise false alarms but miss many real crashes, and even the best agent misses over a quarter of them. Second, locating the code that determines the crash outcome is not enough: agents often misjudge its effect, especially when the crash occurs far from that code. Third, testing only on crashing code is misleading: agents that merely notice suspicious code predict crashes on both source trees, which would look like correct reasoning on the crashing tree alone. Together, these findings indicate that current coding agents cannot yet reliably reason about execution in complex systems codebases, and that paired evaluation is n

papers.title: 5uGUE: Agentic Hardware-in-the-Loop Fuzzing for 5G Devices and beyond
papers.abstract: In this paper, we present 5uGUE, a large language model (LLM)-driven hardware-in-the-loop agent, which enables the wireless fuzzing of 5G-enabled devices (such as mobile phones). 5uGUE combines multi-step reasoning with tool-assisted interaction and integrates into the fuzzing pipeline by leveraging specialized tools for internet search, 5G protocol analysis, memory management, and test-case execution. The agent iteratively generates test cases, executes them on targets, collects runtime feedback, and adaptively refines the fuzzing strategy. We evaluate 5uGUE on five commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) 5G devices across six LLMs. The best performing runs for 5uGUE trigger 167 crashes in total (141 novel and 31 unique) within 60 interaction turns (49 to 133 minutes total runtime). In contrast, the best runs for the state-of-the-art baseline (5GHOUL) discovers only 13 crashes in total (10 novel and 6 unique) within 150 minutes. Overall, by integrating LLM-driven agents, 5uGUE demonstrates significantly better crash discovery performance (12.8x total, 5.2x unique improvement). Notably, our experiments identified 46 unique crashes, 44 of which were confirmed by the vendors but had been previously reported. More importantly, MediaTek confirmed two previously unknown, high-severity vulnerabilities, one of which was assigned CVE-2026-20525. Finally, to demonstrate that 5uGUE is agnostic to wireless protocols, we also extend it to Bluetooth Classic with only minimal code changes. In our

papers.title: ClawMMU: Protection-Coherent Virtual Memory for Stateful LLM Agents
papers.abstract: AI agents keep long-term memory, much of which comes from web pages and tool results. Agent harnesses, the software that runs the model, do not record who may act on this memory, so an instruction hidden in a fetched page can be treated as the user's own instruction. We propose ClawMMU, a protection layer that labels every piece of memory with its owner, scope, origins, and authority. ClawMMU checks these labels whenever content enters the model's context, is written to storage, returns from storage, or drives a tool call. Its central rule is that information may rise in authority, but authority never lifts itself. Because the checks depend on where content came from, not on what it says, memory attacks become classical protection faults that the harness stops even when the model is fooled.

papers.title: CXLResume: Retained-State Checkpoint and Restore for In-Memory Services
papers.abstract: Checkpointing and restoring an in-memory service typically require writing its memory pages to checkpoint images and refilling them at the destination. When application state already resides in shared memory that remains accessible after failover, copying those pages into and out of checkpoint images is unnecessary. We present CXLResume, a prototype that retains the service's main heap objects in shared memory while checkpointing the remaining execution state and mapping metadata. Checkpointing preserves the shared heap at the same freeze point as the serialized process state. During recovery, CXLResume remaps the same shared memory at its original virtual addresses before restoring execution, preserving direct pointers within and across shared and private memory. We evaluate CXLResume with Redis and Memcached using QEMU CXL functional emulation. At 6 GiB, CXLResume reduces combined checkpoint and restore time from 15.015 s to 0.242 s for Redis and from 19.770 s to 0.276 s for Memcached in the evaluated deployments. These results show that retaining shared application state removes large application heaps from the checkpoint data path and substantially reduces checkpoint and restore latency.

papers.title: RPolyPlan: A Unified Global Floorplanning and Legalization Framework for Rectilinear Soft Modules
papers.abstract: Floorplanning with rectilinear soft modules improves area utilization and wirelength by allowing modules to adapt to rectilinear polygon (RPoly) shapes. Existing methods typically construct rectilinear polygons through incremental refinement after obtaining a rectangular global solution, which confines polygon exploration to the neighborhood induced by the initial floorplan. This paper presents RPolyPlan, a unified framework for outline-free and fixed-outline floorplanning that directly incorporates continuously deformable rectilinear polygons into global floorplanning. To enable direct polygon optimization, we introduce a structured continuous representation and a differentiable polygon shaping model that dynamically optimizes rectilinear module shapes based on overlaps, making continuous shape optimization feasible for gradient-based global floorplanning. An augmented Lagrangian formulation robustly handles the coupled inequality constraints, provides theoretical convergence guarantees, and reduces dependence on manual penalty-parameter tuning. During legalization, minimum-cost flow and rectangular decomposition determine the target areas of subrectangles, and horizontal and vertical constraint graphs encode their geometric relations. The resulting convex legalization formulation satisfies the area, shape, separation, connectivity, and outline constraints while minimizing either the chip area or the displacement from the global floorplanning solution. Experiments on the GSR

papers.title: DiffRMST: A GPU-Accelerated Fully Differentiable Rectilinear Minimum Spanning Tree Wirelength Model for Global Placement
papers.abstract: Analytical global placement requires a differentiable wirelength objective that accurately reflects routed interconnect cost. The widely used half-perimeter wirelength (HPWL) is efficient but overlooks the internal topology of multi-pin nets. The rectilinear Steiner minimum tree (RSMT) provides higher fidelity, but its underlying decision problem is NP-complete, and its discrete construction precludes direct use in gradient-based optimization. The rectilinear minimum spanning tree (RMST) offers a polynomial-time alternative, but remains nondifferentiable because of minimization over discrete spanning trees. To address these limitations, we present DiffRMST, a fully differentiable RMST wirelength model for analytical global placement. DiffRMST combines spatial smoothing with a log-sum-exp relaxation to define a continuous distribution over spanning trees. Based on the Kirchhoff matrix-tree theorem, the partition function and edge marginals can be computed without explicit tree enumeration, enabling a closed-form topology-aware gradient for placement optimization. For efficient integration into analytical placement, we further develop a fused forward-backward operator with parallel CPU and GPU implementations. On the ISPD2019 benchmark suite, our method reduces RMST, RSMT, and routed wirelength by an average of 5.0%, 3.2%, and 3.5%, respectively, compared with the weighted-average baseline, while maintaining acceptable runtime. Furthermore, the GPU implementation achieves an av

papers.title: Reinforcement learning for hardware acceleration and system-level optimization on FPGA and integrated-circuit platforms: A survey
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) enables adaptive and autonomous decision-making in embedded, edge, and heterogeneous computing systems. Field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) and integrated circuits (ICs) offer low latency, energy efficiency, and architectural flexibility for RL deployment, while introducing challenges in resource constraints, implementation complexity, and hardware-algorithm co-design. This review surveys more than 100 studies on RL implementations across FPGA and IC platforms, emphasizing architectures, implementation strategies, performance evaluation, and applications. The literature is organized by RL family, including model-based Markov decision processes, classical value-based methods, deep RL, actor-critic, policy-gradient, and multi-agent approaches. We further classify studies by abstraction level, hardware realization strategy, and application domain, examining how RL algorithms map onto reconfigurable and fixed hardware. Unlike surveys restricted to particular algorithms or platforms, this work provides a unified analysis of FPGA and IC implementations, covering acceleration, reconfigurable architectures, energy-aware control, and system-level optimization. Comparative assessments consider resource utilization, latency, throughput, power consumption, and reported performance gains. Finally, we identify recurring architectural patterns, practical limitations, open challenges, and research directions for efficient RL-driven hardware systems. The survey

papers.title: ZKPU: Zero-Knowledge Processing Unit for Heterogeneous Workloads
papers.abstract: Zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs) have become a fundamental building block for privacy-preserving computation, blockchain systems, and verifiable machine learning. Modern ZKP protocols span two distinct families: curve-based protocols, which rely on large finite-field arithmetic, and hash-based protocols, which operate over native 64-bit fields. Existing hardware accelerators are specialized for one protocol family because they are built on operand-scanning Montgomery multiplication, resulting in fixed-width datapaths, poor utilization across heterogeneous operand widths, and limited scalability. This paper presents \emph{ZKPU}, a Zero-Knowledge Processing Unit for heterogeneous ZKP workloads. ZKPU introduces a new compute paradigm by co-designing finely integrated product scanning (FIPS) Montgomery multiplication with a reconfigurable Twin Systolic Fabric (TSF), enabling modular multiplication at arbitrary widths in 64-bit increments. Combined with a fine-grained Deque buffer, on-chip twiddle-factor generator, and memory-efficient MSM preprocessing strategy, ZKPU provides a unified architecture for both curve-based and hash-based protocols. Evaluation using Groth16 and Plonky2 shows that ZKPU achieves up to $144\times$ speedup for NTT, $13.6\times$ for MSM, and approximately $7.2\times$ end-to-end application speedup over state-of-the-art accelerators, while being the first architecture to efficiently support both protocol families on a single reconfigurable hardware platform.

papers.title: KatoANN: Enabling Near-Exact Vector Search at the Speed of Lossy Scans with CPU Matrix Engines
papers.abstract: Distance scans in partition-family approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) search are typically limited by memory bandwidth. Existing systems therefore improve throughput by reading fewer bytes per candidate, often at the cost of recall. We present KatoANN, a CPU ANN search system that removes this tradeoff by batching distance scans on Intel AMX, a CPU matrix engine. Batching allows multiple queries to reuse each fetched vector code, shifting the scan from memory-bound to compute-bound and enabling near-exact distances at the speed of a lossy scan. KatoANN stores each vector once as a 16-bit SQ16 code split into high- and low-byte planes. Its adaptive rank-then-refine scan first ranks all candidates using only the high byte, then refines a small survivor set using the full-byte code. Both stages use the same representation, avoiding a second copy of the raw vectors. Experiments across diverse high-dimensional workloads show that KatoANN is the fastest partition-family ANN search system in our evaluation throughout the high-recall range.

papers.title: Interflow: Breaking the Offline-Online Barrier for Private AI at the Edge
papers.abstract: Privacy-preserving machine learning (PPML) offers a promising path toward bringing powerful AI services to the edge without exposing sensitive user data. However, its practical deployment remains constrained by the high communication, computation, and data-movement costs of secure multi-party computation (MPC), particularly during nonlinear inference. Existing MPC systems typically decouple input-independent correlated randomness generation from online execution, creating substantial memory pressure to buffer single-use cryptographic data. Moreover, limited storage can force a stop-and-refill execution pattern that repeatedly stalls the pipeline to replenish these buffers, bringing randomness generation back onto the critical path. We propose Interflow, an algorithm-hardware co-design that rethinks this separation by batch-wise processing and pipelining correlated-randomness generation with online execution: while the current batch consumes pre-generated randomness to execute secure nonlinear operations, correlation generation proceeds concurrently for the next batch. By leveraging interleaved execution, efficient data movement, and hardware acceleration, the design transforms preprocessing from a serialized, storage-intensive offline phase into a continuously overlapped pipeline that generates correlated randomness closer to the point of consumption, reducing memory footprint and data movement overhead. Implemented on the Zynq UltraScale+ ZCU102, Interflow improves nonlinear

papers.title: Raise or Check? Predicting the Necessity of Additional Fuzzing for Continuous Fuzzing
papers.abstract: Continuous fuzzing is used for vulnerability detection in Open Source Software (OSS). Large-scale services such as Google's OSS-Fuzz fuzz over 1,300 projects and have revealed more than 10,000 vulnerabilities. Despite this, a considerable time lag often exists between when a vulnerability is introduced and when it is detected (i.e., the window of exposure). Given the computational cost of additional fuzzing, we aim to allocate fuzzing resources efficiently using vulnerability-risk estimates. We propose RAISE (Risk-Aware Intensive Supplemental Execution Framework), a Just-In-Time (JIT) framework that prioritizes additional fuzzing for high-risk project-days. RAISE performs binary classification at the project-day granularity to estimate whether a vulnerability is introduced on a given day. We construct a dataset combining vulnerability-introducing commits from the OSV database with daily coverage and change metrics from OSS-Fuzz, covering 15 C/C++ projects and 15,210 project-days, of which 347 (2.28%) are vulnerability-introducing. In a cross-project validation setting, our best model, a Random Forest combining VCCFinder-based static features with dynamic fuzzing features, achieves a ROC-AUC of 0.74, substantially outperforming a random baseline; coverage metrics, led by PatchCoverage, are the most important features. In a simulation over 968 vulnerabilities comparing five allocation strategies, Simple-Regression was significantly more cost-efficient than the prediction-agnost

papers.title: RELAY: Scaling Historical Build Restoration through Rule Reuse and Agentic Repair
papers.abstract: Vulnerability benchmarks and software engineering research depend on rebuilding historical software. Yet builds rely on external resources, such as base images and packages, that change independently of the source code. In this study, we examine this environment decay on 14,159 OSS-Fuzz cases. We find that 69.7% no longer complete reconstruction and verification, and that most failures share a small number of recurring failure symptoms. A recurring failure can therefore be diagnosed once and its repair reused. We present Relay, a hybrid framework that uses an LLM to derive and validate deterministic repair rules from representative failures, reuses them without model calls, and escalates cases unresolved by rules to a per-case agent. We evaluate Relay in human-guided and fully automated rule-derivation campaigns and compare it with a per-case agent approach. We find that rule derivation can be fully automated, and that reusable rules restore as many builds as per-case agents with fewer build executions. However, agents restore cases that the rules cannot. Our results show that a hybrid approach that applies rules first and escalates the remaining cases to an agent restores more builds than either approach alone and at a lower cost than using agents alone.

papers.title: Connection Escrow: Holding AI-Agent Pod Egress in the Kernel Until an Isolated Verifier Rules
papers.abstract: AI agents in containers act by opening network connections, and the text that drives them can be hostile. Controls placed between the agent and its tools are bypassed by a child process or a direct socket, and their approval is not tied to the connection the kernel later opens. We present connection escrow: every outbound TCP connection from a supervised pod is parked inside the kernel's connect() path, before any packet exists, by a 98-instruction eBPF program on the pod's cgroup. A node interceptor attributes the held socket to its kernel socket cookie, process, executable digest, cgroup and pod identity, parks the first bytes the agent writes, and asks a verifier in a separate container with its own key. The connection is released only on a signed verdict naming that one socket cookie and destination, unexpired and unused; no verdict by the deadline resets it, and a late approval is refused. The agent is unmodified. A 36-check adversarial suite with real cgroups passes on the eBPF hold point (33 of the checks also apply, and pass, on an iptables hold point): refused connections never reach the destination; forged, rebound, replayed, expired and late verdicts are refused; the agent's attempt to reach the verifier is itself escrowed; child-process and renamed-binary bypasses fail; UDP is pinned to the resolver. On a Kubernetes cluster, unmodified pods are held per connection and attributed to their SPIFFE identity, a raw socket that bypasses a sidecar proxy is held, and 600

papers.title: Comments Paper: Counterexample for Schedulability Analysis for Self-Suspending Tasks under EDF-Like Scheduling
papers.abstract: This paper provides a counterexample of the sufficient schedulability test for self-suspending real-time tasks under EDF-Like scheduling given by Wang et al. in Theorem 11 of IEEE Transactions on Computers, 74(7):2364-2375, 2025. This paper also shows that their necessary condition is unsound.

papers.title: Green Light: Carbon-Aware Design of Photonic Transformer Accelerators at the Edge
papers.abstract: Migrating transformer inference to the edge requires sustainability considerations that encompass both operation and manufacturing, rather than operational energy alone. Silicon photonics enables high-bandwidth, low-energy matrix multiplication; however, existing microring-resonator-based Dot Product Unit (DPU) organizations have been tailored to convolutional computations and evaluated using analog signaling without accounting for embodied carbon footprints. We adapt three DPU organizations (AMW, MAW, and MWA) to transformer inference workloads and extend each organization to stochastic signaling, yielding six organizations in total. We then calculate their embodied and operational carbon per inference. Across five transformer models and four foundry grids, the photonic system achieves improvements of four, four, and six orders of magnitude in Energy-Delay, Carbon-Delay, and Carbon-Energy Product, respectively, relative to CPUs, while also being compared against H100 SXM5 GPU and TPU v5p baseline systems. Analog-to-stochastic conversion increases die area by 4.3-4.6x and embodied carbon by 4.4-4.8x, while reducing operational energy by approximately 91% and causing embodied carbon to equal or exceed operational carbon per inference. Importantly, the DPU organization and signaling scheme, rather than the foundry grid, are the key determinants of carbon impact. Consequently, the fastest organization (MWA) is not necessarily the most carbon-efficient, whereas MAW-Stochastic off

papers.title: M3D-FLOW: A Monolithic 3-D-Stackable Processing-Near-DRAM Architecture for Generative Normalizing Flow Applications
papers.abstract: Normalizing Flows (NFs) have shown strong results in generative modeling, recently reaching state-of-the-art image generation performance. However, their repetitive, sequential operations limit the computational and memory efficiency achievable with GPUs and TPUs. We propose M3D-FLOW, a novel monolithic 3D-stackable (M3D) DRAM-based processing-near-memory (PNM) architecture that eliminates memory bottlenecks using a Cu-Cu hybrid-bonded logic die integrated with an M3D DRAM die. The M3D DRAM provides dense bank integration and a tiered organization with variable access latencies that M3D-FLOW exploits for the efficient processing of different NF workloads. To maximize compute density while minimizing area, energy, and thermal overhead, M3D-FLOW employs hybrid binary--stochastic floating-point multipliers, performing mantissa multiplication in the stochastic domain and exponent operations in the binary domain. A pipelined execution strategy maps sequential NF stages across dynamically partitioned PE groups, and together with the stochastic hardware, enables M3D-FLOW to achieve at least $6.6\times$ higher performance and $3\times$ better energy efficiency than prior PNM accelerators, with only a 2.2% bits-per-dimension (BPD) increase over bfloat16 and 4.1% over FP32. An analysis of stochastic hardware variants further shows that shorter stochastic bitstreams reduce execution time by up to $3.3\times$ at the cost of higher approximation error, providing a concrete design guide fo

papers.title: Stop Paying by the Letter: Accelerating Full-Chip RTL Simulation with Host-Side Tokenized Logging
papers.abstract: Firmware diagnostic logging (printf) is an essential debug instrument in full-chip SoC design verification, yet it imposes a heavy tax on cycle-accurate RTL simulation: formatting a 30-character, 1-argument message on a simulated CPU and serializing it through an MMIO aperture costs 3.04 to 15.23 $μ$s per call (15.27 $μ$s unweighted / 15.08 $μ$s print-weighted critical-path mean on Suite A). Unlike embedded tokenizers that target flash footprint and wire bytes with offline decoding, RTL simulation is governed by a two-regime cost function---cross-fabric SoC paths are dominated by MMIO bus stalls (84.7% of call latency) whereas local subsystem paths are dominated by on-core vsprintf formatting (61.7%)---and requires live, zero-simulation-time string reconstruction to drive UVM scoreboards. We present a host-side in-simulation tokenized logging architecture for heterogeneous multi-core SoCs that eliminates both bottlenecks with zero firmware call-site edits. Using link-time ELF format-string virtual addresses as tokens over a fixed 32-bit word-aligned slot protocol across Arm, RISC-V, and DSP cores, on-core logging collapses to a single-pass specifier scan and $(1+S)$ MMIO word writes. This removes all on-core radix conversion ($C_{\mathrm{fmt}} \to 0$), 85.0%--94.5% of deployed bus transactions, 84.6%--93.3% of MMIO bus-stall cycles, and 63.5%--90.9% of total on-core logging cycles ($2.74\times$--$11.03\times$), while a SystemVerilog monitor reconstructs bit-exact strings in z

papers.title: Sustainable Processing-in-DRAM Integration and Replacement for Transformer Inference Servers
papers.abstract: Processing-in-DRAM (PID) accelerators are emerging as a sustainable alternative to GPUs for transformer model inference. They bring compute to data, mitigate the memory bandwidth limitation, and reduce the overall energy footprint. Yet, carbon analysis of PID accelerators is covered for only a limited set of hardware and workloads. In this work, we present a carbon modeling framework for PID-enabled inference servers that captures embodied carbon along with idle and active operational carbon. Our evaluation spans three GPU baselines, six PID architectures, and eight transformer workloads. Additionally, we propose an aging-aware model that finds the carbon-optimal replacement period for PID accelerators over a 10-year horizon. Across evaluated configurations, our analysis shows that including PIDs in AI inference servers increases the total embodied carbon by at most 2.5\%, while the total carbon is reduced by up to 1.14$\times$ for encoder and 1.04$\times$ for decoder transformer workloads. The results also depend on GPU selection for pairing, where introducing PID modules in high-end HGX-H100 servers incurs 5.4--5.9$\times$ higher total carbon compared to A100 and H100 servers, due to their larger idle and embodied carbon. Introducing PID modules in higher-end GPU servers, compared to the A100-only baseline, increases (decreases) the total carbon-delay product (CDP) for encoder workloads (decoder workloads).

papers.title: A Combined Streaming FPGA Architecture for Client-Side CKKS Encoding and Encryption
papers.abstract: Homomorphic encryption allows a computing service to process encrypted data, but the client must first encode and encrypt its inputs. Sharing hardware between floating-point encoding and modular encryption reduces area but requires those transform roles to execute at different times. We present a streaming FPGA architecture for CKKS encoding and encryption that computes the shared floating-point encoding transform once and performs the integer transforms for six residue moduli in parallel. Dedicated transform pipelines exchange intermediate results on chip rather than through off-chip memory. DSP Builder generates the transform RTL, and Altera HLS IP Gen compiler compiles the surrounding SYCL pipeline into IP integrated with DMA and control logic in an accelerator functional unit. At polynomial degree N = 8192, the Altera Agilex 7 implementation delivers 5,143 complete ciphertexts per second at 471 MHz. One SEAL-Embedded CPU worker on the same workstation delivers 113 ciphertexts per second for real-valued inputs using all 4,096 slots. Measurements cover prepared-input computation through complete ciphertext construction, including FPGA submission and output delivery.

papers.title: Injection of Space Radiation Errors on Low-power NVM using Generative Deep Learning
papers.abstract: We develop an error model for a Non-Volatile Memory (NVM) device that represents the effects of physical faults experienced in a CubeSat mission in Low Earth Orbit (LEO). The CubeSat carries an off-the-shelf low-power Ferroelectric RAM (FRAM) chip and runs repeated read/write tests according to a predefined pattern. We compare every memory snapshot received from the satellite with a reference bitmap to identify bit errors. We visually analyze erroneous values distributions in the memory snapshots and we understand that they are frequently distributed according to regular spatial patterns. We define a generative deep learning technique to automatically learn these spatial patterns and to synthetically generate additional error patterns mimicking the observed ones. The model is capable at producing memory errors for general application-level experimentation. Our preliminary validation indicates that when comparing the model output with the data we collect, 0.92 of the generated bit flips correspond to bit flips in the memory snapshots and the model captures 0.91 of the observed bit flips. A comparison of the spatial distribution of bit flips in 10,000 generated error patterns also provides a Wasserstein distance of 0.073, indicating that the two distributions differ by roughly 7% of the maximum possible displacement of their probability masses.

papers.title: A Type System for Communication-Safe Hardware Design
papers.abstract: Hardware components communicate through clock-cycle-sensitive protocols. Hardware Description Languages (HDLs), however, provide limited support for expressing these protocols or for checking that independently developed components agree on them. When components disagree, the composed design can perform unsynchronized exchanges or stop making progress. We call these failures communication-safety violations. Communication safety is thus a global property, determined by interactions between components. This makes it difficult to check modularly. This paper presents Pact, a typed extension of Anvil for modular verification of communication safety in synchronous hardware. Pact types describe message-passing, control-flow, and clock-cycle behaviour. Each component is checked against its type. Compatible types guarantee that the components compose into a communication-safe system. Pact also supports incremental design. It can check a subsystem before the rest of the system exists. The check produces a summary type that captures the communication behaviour left for future compositions. To reduce annotation burden, Pact infers types by abstracting payload values while preserving communication, timing, control, and fairness. These inferred types are optimal for the checker: whenever some checker-accepted types can prove compatibility, the inferred types can prove it as well. Type inference and type checking are decidable, and compatibility is decided by a sound and complete algorithm.

papers.title: A 105 MS/s 4.18 nJ/inference 0.765 $\text{mm}^\text{2}$ Mixed-Signal Streaming ML Engine for Wireless Baseband in 12LP+ FinFET
papers.abstract: We present SIXPPAC, the first streaming machine-learning engine for real-time integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) in wireless systems. SIXPPAC integrates two SAR ADCs and a digital binary-weight six-layer neural network (NN). The 0.765 mm$^\text{2}$ 12 nm FinFET engine stores all NN parameters on chip, enabling sustained 105 MS/s processing of 8b I/Q baseband samples at 0.8 V. By deploying bipolar inner products using AND instead of XNOR gates, SIXPPAC consumes 4.18 nJ/inference (0.42 POPS/W) at 0.8 V. We evaluate SIXPPAC on three example applications to demonstrate its versatility.

papers.title: Multi-Agent AI Design of a Nanowatt Biomedical Low-Pass Filter from Topology to Layout
papers.abstract: We demonstrate a multi-agent framework that takes an analog circuit from topology synthesis to layout. A researcher agent directs schematic and layout agents, a four-tier memory stores the specification and lessons, and separate agents review the designs. Deterministic tools provide pass/fail simulation reports, symbolic analysis, graph-based netlist equivalence, parasitic injection, and extraction with DRC and LVS in every optimization trial. A human approves the specification and the layout plan. For a fourth-order, 250-Hz subthreshold biopotential low-pass filter, the researcher agent synthesized, through simulation-guided trial and error, a novel current-reuse architecture that shares a single dc bias branch between a super-source-follower biquad and a flipped-voltage-follower biquad.
