The agents completed a DRC- and LVS-clean layout in 130-nm IHP SG13G2 CMOS that meets the specification in nominal post-layout simulation, despite the noise-power trade-off and threshold-voltage sensitivity of subthreshold operation. The filter's input-referred noise over 0.5-200 Hz is 41.6% below that of the super-source-follower reference design at about equal core power.

papers.title: E-Layout: Layout-Stage Logic Restructuring via RL-Optimized Equality-Saturated Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.abstract: Achieving high sign-off performance in advanced ICs increasingly depends on layout-stage optimization under realistic physical conditions. While recent efforts have moved toward synthesis-layout fusion, most existing works still focus on bringing estimated physical information earlier into synthesis, whose optimization does not fully correlate with real layout-stage behavior. Meanwhile, layout-stage optimization remains largely restricted to a fixed logic structure, relying mainly on buffering and sizing. This fundamentally constrains the optimization space under realistic physical conditions. To address this, we present E-Layout, an ML-driven framework for post-placement layout restructuring. E-Layout jointly optimizes logic transformation and physical implementation across multiple subcircuits under design-level timing feedback. This enables the selection of the most timing-beneficial set of disjoint restructured subcircuits to form the optimized circuit. Specifically, it first constructs equivalence-preserving logic alternatives via e-graph equality saturation, then couples logic selection with physical realization through a graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) model, and finally refines these local logic-physical decisions with reinforcement learning under design-level timing feedback. Evaluated on 9 diverse designs, it achieves on average 6% TNS improvement and 2% WNS improvement, while even reducing area by 1%, over an industry-leading commercial physical de

papers.title: A Generic On-Board AI Processing Chain for Earth Observation: From Application Development to Embedded Deployment and Mission-Level Orchestration
papers.abstract: Earth observation satellites acquire more data than they can downlink. Extracting information on board with artificial intelligence (AI) turns the satellite into a data-reduction stage that downlinks compact products, such as masks or detections, instead of full scenes; deploying it in a mission, however, involves the whole processing chain and not only the neural network. We present a generic on-board AI processing chain along three axes, with wildfire segmentation as the worked example among ship detection and cloud segmentation. (i) The AI model is tuned (spectral-band selection, input normalization), quantized to 8-bit integers (int8) and ported to an AMD Versal VCK190, with its excellent segmentation performance preserved on the board. (ii) A modular tiler-inference-mosaicer workflow, reused unchanged across applications, brings the tile-level model to scene level, turning a full acquisition into a scene-level mask or detection list. (iii) Each step is packaged as a unikernel and orchestrated on board by ORCHIDE, a cloud-native orchestrator. The chain is characterized end to end, from the standalone execution on the target to its execution under orchestration with parallel workflows on a representative test bench. Beyond AI inference on individual tiles, this approach aims at increasing the maturity of on-board AI deployment by addressing a complete processing chain, from the acquired scene to the mission-level execution.

papers.title: VHDLBench: Benchmarking and Fine-Tuning Large Language Models for VHDL-Based Chip Design
papers.abstract: The rapid evolution of digital circuit complexity demands innovative approaches to hardware design automation. While Large Language Models (LLMs) have influenced software development, their application to Hardware Description Language (HDL) generation remains largely unexplored, particularly for VHDL. This paper presents a comprehensive study for AI-assisted digital circuit design, addressing gaps in current Electronic Design Automation workflows. The work introduces a VHDL dataset of 18,500+ syntax-verified examples from open-source repositories and converted Verilog designs. Five 7B-parameter LLMs were fine-tuned using parameter-efficient QLoRA technique, enabling deployment in resource-constrained environments. To evaluate model efficacy, a rigorous three-level pipeline was established: (1) syntax and synthesis validation, (2) functional simulation with testbenches, and (3) FPGA prototyping on Zynq SoCs. Results show fine-tuned models achieve up to 92% syntax correctness and 73% functional accuracy on common design tasks, with DeepSeek-Coder demonstrating the highest performance gains. Generated designs were successfully deployed on real hardware, confirming not only syntactic but operational viability. This work demonstrates that LLMs, when tailored with domain-specific data and lightweight fine-tuning can contribute meaningfully to the future of generative EDA workflows.

papers.title: A Hybrid GPU and Processing-Near-Memory Architecture with Shared DRAM for Efficient Prefill-Decode Disaggregation
papers.abstract: The growing adoption of large language models (LLMs) has significantly increased the compute and memory demands of inference serving. A key challenge arises from the mismatch between compute-bound prefill and memory-bound decoding: when executed together, the two phases interfere, while separating them via prefill-decode (PD) disaggregation leads to substantial resource underutilization. Specifically, prefill leaves memory bandwidth underutilized, whereas decoding underutilizes compute resources. Prior approaches, such as GPU Streaming Multiprocessor (SM) partitioning, attempt to improve utilization by spatially dividing GPU resources. However, these approaches remain fundamentally limited, as memory-bound decoding still requires a large number of SMs to saturate bandwidth, reducing the compute resources available for prefill and resulting in an inherent trade-off. To address this limitation, we propose DuoPD, a hybrid PD-disaggregation architecture that integrates lightweight Processing-Near-Memory (PNM) units into the HBM logic die. Unlike prior PIM/PNM designs that rely on costly internal bandwidth scaling and offload only partial decoding operations, DuoPD enables full decoding execution on PNM by leveraging bandwidth sharing with the GPU over a shared HBM interface. This allows compute-bound prefill and memory-bound decoding to execute concurrently with minimal interference, improving both compute and memory utilization. To realize this design, we develop a compact PNM m

papers.title: Superposed analog memory for vector storage in neural networks
papers.abstract: The growing memory demands of artificial neural networks pose a major challenge for energy-efficient computing, particularly for models that rely on large collections of high-dimensional weight and embedding vectors. Conventional memory architectures store these vectors individually, requiring many memory cells per vector and limiting achievable storage density. Here we demonstrate an analog memory architecture that encodes multiple vectors in a distributed superposition within a single memory array. Individual vectors are recovered through in-memory matrix-vector multiplication, allowing the degree of superposition to be tuned to balance storage density against recall fidelity. This approach introduces a new scaling dimension for analog memory, in which effective storage density can be increased without a corresponding increase in the number of physical memory cells. The distributed representation also provides resilience to device-level noise. We implement the architecture on a prototype phase-change memory chip and experimentally evaluate it using embedding tables from deep learning recommendation models and large language models. The results demonstrate inference accuracy comparable to full-precision software baselines, establishing analog superposition as a promising route towards dense, energy-efficient memory for artificial intelligence.

papers.title: MX-Like Tensor Core for LLM Inference with NPU Integration via Hardware-Software Co-Design Exploration
papers.abstract: Block-scaled quantization formats such as OCP Microscaling (MX) and NVFP4 have been widely adopted as efficient data formats for LLM inference. However, the design space of these formats spanned by shared scale, weight, and activation format combinations has not been systematically explored, and the joint accuracy-silicon tradeoff across this space remains uncharacterized, leaving the true Pareto-optimal configurations for NPU-based edge LLM deployment an open question. To bridge this gap, we conduct a joint hardware-software (HW-SW) co-design exploration of the above underexplored MX-like design space with three innovations. 1) We define and systematically characterize the full 8-bit scale format family within the MX-like design space, jointly with asymmetric weight-activation precision, identifying configurations that outperform the MX and NVFP4-like (without per-tensor scaling, PTS) baselines. 2) We build a per-format specialized MAC datapath template that enables fair hardware cost evaluation across the space. 3) We develop an automated co-design flow, integrated into the open-source SNAX NPU platform, that enables joint HW-SW analysis across the design space. Overall, our co-design exploration reveals that scale format matters only under aggressive FP4 quantization, yielding a case-oriented design guideline for both scale format and asymmetric weight-activation precision. We further identify UE5M3 as a favorable accuracy-hardware tradeoff for the FP4 regime, reducing per

papers.title: 3D-MoE: Complementarity-Guided Hardware-Software Co-Design for MoE Decode on 3D-Stacked NMP
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) have become a mainstream way to scale Large Language Models (LLMs), because each token activates only a small subset of experts, reducing inference cost. However, MoE decode remains highly memory-bound and exhibits strongly skewed, time-varying expert loads. 3D-stacked DRAM near-memory processing (NMP) provides the bandwidth that decode demands, yet its tiled organization makes load balancing expensive: expert parallelism (EP) preserves locality but suffers from hotspot-induced imbalance, while more distributed strategies weaken locality and increase NoC traffic. To address this locality-balance conflict, we observe that domain-specialized token routing creates offsetting expert-load fluctuations across decode steps, a property we call expert complementarity. Using this insight, we propose 3D-MoE, a hardware--software co-designed system for MoE decode on 3D-stacked NMP. 3D-MoE uses offline, one-time complementarity-guided grouping and locality-aware mapping to establish coarse-grained inter-group balance, handles residual intra-group hotspots through a lightweight Collaborative Memory-Network (CMN) that streams each hot expert's weight tiles once from its host DRAM channel to helper cores over a reconfigured local broadcast path, and uses cost-aware online remapping to remain robust to workload drift. Across MoE models, 3D-MoE achieves an average 4.63$\times$ MoE-layer speedup over EP and improves end-to-end throughput by 1.58$\times$--1.86$\times$ ov

papers.title: Learn the Interface, Not the Implementation: Output Representation Dominates Training Regime in LLM-Based RTL Generation
papers.abstract: Large-language-model register-transfer-level (RTL) generation has concentrated on how to train the model: fine-tuning, continued pre-training, and reinforcement learning from a verifier. We argue this is the second-order question. On a bounded, formally specifiable task of generating single-error-correcting, double-error-detecting (SECDED) ECC memory wrappers, we hold the task, data, and correctness oracle fixed and vary two axes independently: the training regime (seven settings) and the output representation (four levels, from fully expanded flat Verilog to an eight-field configuration expanded by a deterministic generator). Because a reference generator exists, correctness is decided by formal equivalence over a design space of approximately ten million points, rather than sampled from a hand-written testbench. Two results follow. First, representation dominates: every representation close to raw RTL reaches a pass rate of at most 0.17, while the configuration reaches 0.83 with no training at all. Once the model emits the configuration, every training regime achieves a pass rate between 0.89 and 1.00. Second, raw RTL hits a hard output-length limit: a 512-bit design requires 44,237 tokens of flat Verilog compared with just 69 tokens for the configuration. Consequently, raw generation becomes infeasible above 32-bit data words rather than merely inaccurate. A model trained from scratch with fewer than 50 million parameters, combined with the verified generator, achieves 0.8

papers.title: AgentLens: Framework-Aware Characterization and Resource Control for Heterogeneous LLM Agents
papers.abstract: LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed on shared hosts, yet their host-side resource demands remain poorly understood, limiting effective resource coordination. We present AgentLens, which combines a cross-framework workload characterization with a framework-aware resource controller for co-located agents. Across 10 frameworks and 11 matched coding tasks, we find that framework orchestration strongly shapes resource demand: framework identity explains 52.95% of peak RSS variance, compared with 4.22% for task identity, while execve events per tool call differ by 39x between MetaGPT and CAMEL. Resource dimensions are not interchangeable: peak RSS and subprocess count have a Spearman correlation of 0.13. Static budgets and framework-agnostic policies miss these structural differences and the alternation between API waiting and tool execution. AgentLens combines offline framework fingerprints with online execution-phase signals to coordinate memory through cgroup v2, without modifying framework internals. In trace-driven replay across three co-location pairs at a memory budget of 90% of aggregate peak demand, AgentLens keeps the protected worker's P95 allocation latency at 5.7-7.1 ms, improving on static allocation by 2.1-2.6x.

papers.title: gKSM: GPU Memory Deduplication at Driver Layer for Serverless LLM Inference
papers.abstract: In serverless LLM inference, cloud providers commonly locate multiple instances on a single GPU to improve utilization. However, each instance independently maintains its model weights and runtime state, making duplicate GPU memory the primary bottleneck. Memory deduplication is a widely-used technique for eliminating duplicate data in CPU systems, but extending it to GPU memory faces fundamental challenges. Effective GPU memory deduplication must avoid redundant data movement between CPU and GPU while preserving write isolation for shared pages without native copy-on-write (COW) support. This paper presents gKSM, a transparent GPU memory deduplication framework for serverless LLM inference. gKSM addresses these challenges through CPU-GPU collaborative hash management that offloads hash computation to GPU kernels, zero-copy model weight deduplication that eliminates duplication before model weight transfer, and a cross-privilege page fault handler that combines a lightweight kernel hook and CUDA Virtual Memory Management (VMM) remapping in the user space. gKSM also designs a stable page scanning algorithm and a reuse-aware placement policy in cluster scale. Experiments show that gKSM reduces GPU memory usage by 59.8% while maintaining high throughput compared to ServerlessLLM. Under memory constrained workloads, gKSM improves aggregate throughput by 2.15X and supports five instances concurrently. In cluster level simulation, gKSM achieves a service rate of 99.97%, compared to

papers.title: Visual Cache Reuse for Efficient Multimodal Inference
papers.abstract: Vision-language model (VLM) inference incurs substantial prefill latency and memory overhead due to the long visual token sequences of large visual inputs. Existing serving systems typically exploit exact cache reuse through prefix caching or position-independent caching, overlooking the potential of approximate caching in real-world workloads. However, directly reusing an approximate cache entry may introduce spurious visual information, which naive approaches that select a subset of important visual tokens for recomputation fail to adequately mitigate this risk. We present VisMemo, an efficient serving system that enables approximate KV cache reuse for modern VLMs. Its core is a system-algorithm co-design that combines an entropy-aware KV cache reuse algorithm with differentiated cache management. Specifically, VisMemo uses patch entropy to identify reuse candidates and warmup attention to prioritize recomputation based on the current query. To support the large cache capacity across GPU memory, CPU memory, and SSD storage, VisMemo applies distinct I/O and cache policies to exact and approximate hits: sparse patch-level I/O for approximate hits, prioritized retention for exact hits, and a reserved CPU victim cache for preset entries selected using offline workload priors and online reuse observations. VisMemo further optimizes the memory access path between the inference engine and the storage backend, eliminating redundant caching and unnecessary data movement. Experiments

papers.title: Heuristic-Driven Resource Optimization for Decoupled Memory Channels on FPGAs
papers.abstract: Determining OpenCL channel depths for Decoupled Access-Execute (DAE) architectures in High-Level Synthesis (HLS) is critical for balancing performance and hardware efficiency. Conventional static analysis tools often over-provision these memory channels to ensure performance safety, leading to significant resource stranding. This paper presents an expansion of an LLVM-based static analysis framework, originally proposed for automated DAE generation, by introducing a hardware-aware refinement layer. We identify a counter-intuitive Performance Inversion Paradox linked to baseline memory stalls, where high-stall, grid-based kernels reach peak performance at minimal channel depths and suffer up to a 61% throughput degradation when depths are increased. We propose a Heuristic Refinement Layer that optimizes OpenCL channel depths based on this correlation between baseline stalls and performance saturation. Experimental results demonstrate that our expanded framework successfully identifies the Minimal Peak Performance point across various benchmarks. By avoiding the performance traps of standard over-provisioning, we achieve a 2.52x improvement in Resource Efficiency for an illustrative HotSpot application. This approach maintains peak execution speedup while ensuring the leanest possible hardware profile, outperforming conservative tool-based static predictions.

papers.title: Cryogenic Recharacterization of a Commercial 22 nm FD-SOI Foundry Standard-Cell Library
papers.abstract: Wiring and bandwidth bottlenecks between a quantum processor and room-temperature electronics can be reduced by placing digital control at the cryogenic stage, but commercial foundry standard-cell libraries are not specified for operation at 4 K. A cryogenic recharacterization flow is therefore developed for a commercial 22 nm FD-SOI foundry standard-cell library using commercially available cryogenic compact-device models, while retaining the original cell circuits, layouts, logic functions, and implementation semantics and remaining compatible with the commercial synthesis, place-and-route, and signoff methodology used at room temperature. Body-bias dependence is quantified over 38,640 matched slew/load points at zero, +/-0.9 V, and +/-1.8 V body bias. Relative to full bias, zero-bias operation increases the median rising and falling delays by 38.6x and 33.0x, while approximately 90% of transitions exceed the foundry-defined maximum-transition envelope. The 0.8 V-to-0.4 V level shifter is even more sensitive to body bias: its worst-case falling delay decreases from 30.6 ns at zero bias to 0.56 ns at +/-1.8 V. For the outbound 0.4 V-to-0.8 V crossing, driving the 0.8 V receiver without a level shifter dissipates 57.7 uW of static power per bit at full bias, against 0.196 nW when level-shifted. In post-route analysis of the unchanged extracted physical database of a fabricated 32-bit ALU, the register-to-register setup boundary increases from 1.3 MHz at zero bias to 37.9 MHz

papers.title: Accelerating CPU Speculative Decoding via Unified Graph Execution and Transactional KV Isolation
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM inference, but deploying it on CPUs introduces severe systems bottlenecks: context-swapping latency between draft and target graphs, and memory allocation overhead during KV cache rollbacks. We introduce SubTernary, an execution framework that eliminates these costs through Unified Graph Caching and Transactional KV-Cache Isolation. By compiling both models into a single memory arena with a persistent thread pool and routing speculative tokens to a static scratchpad for zero-copy pointer resets, SubTernary avoids dynamic reallocation and thread synchronization entirely. We integrate a 256-bit AVX2 ternary SIMD kernel as a low-bit case study. Ablations reveal our systems runtime drives 35.0% of the throughput gains, while the ternary kernel adds 6.0%. SubTernary achieves a $1.35\times$ speedup over llama.cpp speculative decoding and $3.99\times$ over autoregressive decoding, maintaining $O(1)$ rollback latency.

papers.title: Who Verifies the Builder? Toward Independent Assurance for Agent-Produced Software
papers.abstract: Coding agents can now implement a specification, write and run tests, repair failures, and declare the result ready for release. When the same agentic system produces both the software and the evidence of its correctness, a passing test suite is no longer independent evidence: visible tests become an optimization target, code and tests may share one misinterpretation of the specification, and the builder's own tests may simply be incomplete. This paper argues that agent-produced software requires an assurance plane that is structurally independent of the build plane. We characterize four gaps between stakeholder intent and production (requirement, conformance, evaluation, and model gaps) and identify which of them verification can close. We propose a framework that separates building from verifying, introduces a Verification Contract stating what must be demonstrated before release, and organizes verification in a specification-first phase without access to the implementation and an implementation-aware phase based on mutation analysis, property-based testing, and fuzzing, with an assurance report that leaves the release decision to a human. We evaluate the framework in a pre-registered study on three stateful services, two of them written by third-party models, and an EvalPlus pilot. The builder's programs were correct, but its own tests missed subtle interactions: a verifier in a fresh context detected more of the 46 seeded faults than the builder's tests (Holm-corrected p

papers.title: Leveraging verifiable structure in quantum circuits to find more efficient compilations with agentic AI
papers.abstract: We discuss an effective paradigm of utilizing AI agents to better compile quantum circuits when one can constrain bottleneck subroutines to have some form of classically verifiable structure. For example, when critical subroutines are composed exclusively of reversible classical logic, phasing operations, and measurement based uncomputation, one can efficiently simulate execution for classical inputs. This property facilitates efficient certification of approximate circuit synthesis via a form of fuzz testing, provided suitable assumptions on the input distribution. While this pattern was recently exploited to improve quantum cryptanalysis circuits, here we highlight the flexibility of the broader approach by discussing three important applications. (1) The computation of $1/\sqrt{x}$ that bottlenecks real space simulations of the Coulomb operator such as those important for modeling inertial confinement fusion reactors. (2) The decoding of Reed-Solomon codes which bottlenecks the decoded quantum interferometry algorithm when used to approximately solve the optimal polynomial intersection problem. And (3) the quantum look-up tables and controlled application of Givens rotations that bottleneck the most performant quantum algorithms for simulating chemistry in second quantization. We discuss reference implementations of these algorithms and how they can be constrained and verified in the interest of seeding a Kaggle competition designed to accelerate AI-based research into the

papers.title: AgentLoupe: Kernel-Resident Semantic Causal Labels for AI Agent Observability
papers.abstract: AI agents translate user intents into system actions via tool invocations. Accurately attributing these actions to their originating LLM interactions is essential for security auditing, yet existing methods, such as AgentSight, fail for delayed execution and cross-process-lineage behaviors. We present AgentLoupe, an application-transparent eBPF-based observability tool. The core insight of AgentLoupe is to embed causal identity into kernel resources. AgentLoupe employs eBPF to capture TLS plaintext to interpret LLM interactions, and assigns each a kernel-resident semantic label. It maintains labels in eBPF maps, then propagates this label across processes and threads, associates it with kernel resources such as files and sockets. When a persistent resource carries context to an independent process outside the original lineage, this design preserves the delayed causal association. Experiments show that the average observation overhead of AgentLoupe is below 8%, and case studies confirm AgentLoupe traces cross-lineage persistent attacks back to their originating LLM interactions.

papers.title: FuzzInsight: Navigating the Efficiency-Effectiveness Trade-off in Coverage-Guided DNN Fuzzing
papers.abstract: Collecting and labeling diverse test datasets for evaluating Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) is costly and time-consuming. This has motivated coverage-guided fuzzing techniques that generate defect-revealing corner cases from limited test data. However, their effectiveness depends heavily on configuration choices, particularly coverage criteria and seed-selection strategies. We present a configuration-oriented analysis and decision guidelines for scalable DNN fuzzing targeting two bottlenecks: inefficient seed utilization and the cost of coverage guidance. Our analysis shows that existing seed-selection strategies repeatedly prioritize a small subset of inputs, leaving many collected seeds unexplored. To address this issue, we propose Equalized Sampling, a constraint-based strategy that increases mean seed queue utilization to 77%, improving on prior approaches by 13 percentage points. We further evaluate 84 fuzzing configurations on four benchmark datasets: MNIST, SVHN, GTSRB, and CIFAR-100. Results show that the non-structural criteria LSCD, LSC, and MDSC achieve coverage outcomes comparable to structural and alternative non-structural criteria while requiring substantially less computation. These criteria also promote broad behavioral exploration of the DNN under test, reducing the need to monitor multiple coverage metrics. Among them, LSCD provides a modest but consistent runtime advantage. Finally, we show that retraining with generated corner cases improves generalization r

papers.title: Efficient Program Reduction for Library Fuzzing Harnesses
papers.abstract: Library fuzzing harnesses translate generated inputs into API calls. When a complex harness triggers a crash, developers must determine whether the cause is a library defect or invalid harness usage. A smaller reproducer can simplify this investigation, but obtaining one requires repeatedly building and executing modified harnesses and analyzing their crashes, making manual or even automatic minimization time-consuming. Moreover, data-dependent statements prevent the reducer to remove unnecessary code and the heavy stack trace symbolization in libraries also slows down the candidate execution. To address these challenges, we present HarnessMinimizer, a system for efficient minimization of C/C++ library fuzzing harnesses. Its optimized pipeline reuses header analysis and prepared libraries and runtimes to reduce the work required to build and execute each simplified harness during the reduction process. It records and replays input values so that unnecessary input operations can be removed without changing the values supplied to surviving calls. It also uses a fast method to check whether each simplified harness preserves the original crash, avoiding repeated stack trace symbolization. We evaluate HarnessMinimizer with four reduction engines on 200 crash cases from 21 open source libraries. Compared with the unoptimized pipeline, HarnessMinimizer achieves speedups of 3.46-4.51 times in average total wall time. Average harness size decreases from 1,352 original tokens to 143-26

papers.title: Characterizing Predictability-Latency Trade-offs of KV-Cache SSD Offloading in LMCache for LLM Serving Systems
papers.abstract: KV-cache offload is widely used to stretch GPU memory for LLM serving, but its storage behavior has not been characterized at the block-device level. In this paper, we study LMCache through realworld multi-session workloads that span same/different context x same/different prompt, using over 100 stateless requests per workload. Our comparison is observational rather than factorial: it contrasts two realizable deployment snapshots -- LMCache 0.3.0 with buffered I/O and the kernel page cache, and LMCache 0.3.16 with prefix-aware deduplication and O_DIRECT. Key findings define the paper. First, the legacy stack appears almost read-free at the SSD layer in all four workloads, but a flush_ram experiment shows that this is conditional on page-cache warmth: once the cache is evicted, the same path issues about 1 GB of sequential reads in 683 ms. Second, deduplication delivers a dramatic write reduction only for the exact-repeat workload: one set collapses from 1.62 GB to 11.75 MB of writes, while the other three sets remain in the 2-5 GB range. Third, O_DIRECT converts a hidden and bimodal read cost into an explicit and stable one: on one set, warm TTFT rises from 27 ms to 93 ms because each of the 99 warm requests re-reads the same ~12 MB partial chunk from SSD. The main conclusion is therefore not "newer is better," but a system trade-off: predictability versus average-case latency.

papers.title: Range: Decoupling KV-Cache Reuse Granularity from Storage Work
papers.abstract: LLM serving reuses cached key-value (KV) state to skip prefill, and growing contexts push that state past GPU HBM and CPU DRAM onto NVMe SSDs, placing prefix restore on the critical path of time-to-first-token (TTFT). We find that on a well-configured host-issued path the SSD is not the bottleneck: restoring the same 6 GiB of KV takes 2.1 s as 192 objects but 3.0 s as 6,144 objects, and more under layerwise loading, because every layer of the storage stack - lookup, allocation, I/O submission, GPU delivery, store, index - charges per logical object while the bytes stay the same. This cost grows with the KV footprint: longer contexts, deeper models under layerwise loading, and tensor parallelism each multiply the object count. Prior systems move this per-object work from the CPU to the GPU; the work remains per object. This paper presents Range, a KV-cache storage engine for vLLM and LMCache built on one principle: every cost on the storage path scales with bytes or physical batches, never with logical objects. Range tickets replace per-key lookup and ownership with token metadata and physical leases; byte stripes make the on-media layout independent of reuse granularity; completion-owned GPU transfer banks batch delivery and extraction and release each layer to attention as it lands. Range keeps the kernel cuFile path and changes four lines of vLLM. On a fixed 6 GiB restore, Range's median TTFT stays at 1.79-1.80 s across a 32x range of object counts and under layerwise deliv

papers.title: Where the SRAM Goes: Per-Symbol Attribution of Static Memory in FreeRTOS-C and Embassy-Rust IoT Firmware on a 64 KB RISC-V Microcontroller
papers.abstract: Selecting a firmware stack for a memory-constrained microcontroller is usually guided by aggregate binary sizes, which report how much SRAM a build consumes but not where it goes or why. We address that gap with a per-symbol attribution method that decomposes static RAM into architectural categories - scheduler heap, network buffers and pools, task stacks, and linker-reserved regions - by bounding sized ELF symbols to the .data, .bss and .stack section ranges. The method is validated by reconciling every category sum exactly against the size-based totals for all sixteen builds. We apply it to eight cumulative firmware milestones, from a bare task scaffold to a full MQTT-over-Ethernet client, implemented twice, in FreeRTOS-C and in Embassy-Rust, on the CH32V203RBT6, a RISC-V microcontroller with 64 KB SRAM and an on-chip Ethernet MAC and PHY, with functional parity verified on hardware at every milestone. The decomposition shows that both stacks spend a nearly identical share of their RAM on networking (63.8% versus 63.9%), yet the absolute cost differs by 4.4 times: 40,719 bytes for lwIP against 9,316 bytes for smoltcp. FreeRTOS task stacks grow linearly at roughly 1 KB per task while Embassy async state grows with state-machine complexity. We also report that lwIP could not be integrated under an all-static discipline on this platform, requiring a 20 KB arena that smoltcp does not. The measurement harness, the attribution tool, and the sixteen firmware implementations are re

papers.title: Exact Makespan Bounds and the GPipe Homogeneity Bias for Heterogeneous LLM Inference Pipelines
papers.abstract: We give an exact critical-path characterization of the makespan of micro-batch pipelines serving LLMs on heterogeneous GPU clusters, quantifying how the classic homogeneous GPipe formula errs. In the pure-forward, communication-free, infinite-buffer setting, T(M) = (M-1)tau_max + Sum_j tau_j, where tau_j is stage j's per-micro-batch service time and M the micro-batch count (Theorem 1). Under asynchronous communication -- modern NCCL-based serving -- it extends to T(M) = Sum_j tau_j + Sum_j d_j + (M-1)tau_max, with Sum_j d_j a purely additive constant (Theorem 2); under blocking communication, T(M) = (M-1)sigma_max + Sum_s sigma_s with sigma_s = tau_s + d_s, so communication enters the steady-state slope iff some d_s > tau_max - tau_s (Theorem 3). These results quantify the GPipe overestimate, decompose the bias into a homogeneity term Sum_j (tau_max - tau_j) and a communication-ignoring term Sum_j d_j, and imply that balancing per-stage compute dominates communication reduction for steady-state throughput. A real system with partial overlap is sandwiched between Theorems 2 and 3, with a closed-form bound on the overlap throughput gain. All claims are validated pointwise (error < 10^-9) on eleven configurations and a 1.6x10^5-point fuzz, including a mixed RTX 5090/3090/GTX 1070 partition. We situate the results in flow-shop scheduling and list open extensions: bandwidth-limited communication, bounded buffers, prefill-decode interleaving.

papers.title: HPCAgent-Bench: A Framework for Sound Benchmarking of Code-Optimizing Agents, Harnesses, and Skills
papers.abstract: Coding agents are increasingly used to optimize code, but existing benchmarks fix one accelerator, programming model or harness, so they cannot isolate what each component contributes or show whether added skills and tools repay their cost. We present HPCAgent-Bench with 689 kernels in three tracks: loop-level optimization challenges, kernels extracted from HPC codes, and machine-learning models. The framework specifies each kernel once in NumPy, derives C and Fortran references, accepts submissions through a common C ABI or Python interface, and runs them on CPUs or GPUs, on one or multiple nodes. An external judge checks correctness on hidden fuzzed inputs and times each submission, closing paths agents use to exploit the testing system. We introduce two metrics for reporting results: \textit{intervention efficacy} measures an intervention, such as adding a tool, through paired runs on speedup, success rate and cost, and \textit{weighted token cost} reports input, cached-input and output tokens under explicit weights. Agents reach up to $4.2\times$ speedup over automatic parallelizers, and their optimizations transfer to another machine: $93$--$99\%$ of answers without device-specific code remain correct, and per-kernel speedups keep a rank correlation of $r_s\ge0.84$. Across 40 matched setups, interventions significantly change speedup only twice but token cost by up to $3.0\times$. Because token weighting decides whether a saving is significant, we state the weights and r

papers.title: Towards Virtual Networking for a Time-Triggered Hypervisor
papers.abstract: Virtualization enables mixed-criticality applications to run on shared hardware by isolating them within separate virtual machines (VMs). However, achieving end-to-end timing guarantees for critical tasks hosted on virtual CPUs (VCPUs) without relying on static partitioning is hard. A possible solution is a time-triggered hypervisor that dispatches VMs' VCPUs to processor cores according to a predetermined global schedule. A global schedule includes the computation, the network, and the virtualization layer to provide end-to-end timing guarantees across hosts and VMs during design time. In this work, we propose a VirtIO-based virtual network that realizes IEEE 802.1Qbv quasi-compliant inter-VM communication, providing predictable timing for critical messages exchanged between time-triggered VMs. We present our VirtIO-based virtual network architecture and derive network-level scheduling constraints that emerge from the properties of the proposed solution. We implement the proposed design in the ACRN hypervisor and evaluate the end-to-end latency of critical traffic in a loaded network, demonstrating that our time-triggered VirtIO-net prototype provides predictable end-to-end latency under load.

papers.title: Memorix: Managing Memory Selections for AI Agents
papers.abstract: AI agents now handle a growing share of tasks across sessions within a persistent project. Their behavior depends not only on the model, but heavily on the persistent state they read from the environment. Existing systems assemble this memory at use time, splicing selected files into the prompt as a one-off payload. As a result, per-task assembly is costly and can still miss critical material, failures cannot be traced or replayed, and agents can read documentation written for the wrong version. Our key insight is that what an agent should read is mostly determined by its project, so the selection can be computed once, ahead of time, and reused across tasks. We propose Memorix, an agent memory system that realizes this insight. Memorix achieves this via three key mechanisms: (1) an immutable and versioned Store pins every source by identity and reproduces historical layouts cheaply, (2) a View that splits selection (Derivations) from composition (Environment), making the result reproducible and shareable, and (3) Quests and Profiles keep a delivered view refreshable and available inside the project as sources evolve. We implement Memorix and evaluate it on SWE-ContextBench and LibEvolutionEval against mainstream agent memory systems. Precomputed Environments raise resolved rate by up to 1.5X and deliver the correct library version on every version-conditioned task, while cutting amortized cost by up to 100X and build time by up to 38X.

papers.title: SolBehave: Evaluating the Behavioural Correctness of LLM-Generated Smart Contracts
papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly generate Solidity smart contracts that, once deployed, can never be patched, making a single latent fault permanent and exploitable. Yet current evaluations mostly ask only whether generated code compiles. We introduce SolBehave, a benchmark for evaluating the correctness of model-generated contracts at scale, moving beyond ad hoc unit tests. Across 250 real, reproducible Ethereum contracts, we apply three complementary tests of behavioural fidelity: differential fuzzing, historical-transaction replay, and, as our core contribution, synthetic-transaction replay guided by a Dynamic Condition Response (DCR) graph that enumerates the space of legitimate function-call sequences. Differential fuzzing compares each generated function with the original on automatically generated inputs; historical replay compares the whole contract on the transactions it actually received on-chain; DCR-guided replay compares it on sequences of calls that follow its intended usage, including orderings that never occurred on-chain. We evaluate seven state-of-the-art open-weight models after one round of automated repair. Compilation success ranges from 26.4% to 92.7%, but under differential fuzzing only 31.4% of all generated function bodies that compile, pooled over models and samples, are equivalent to the original. Divergence at the contract level is the norm rather than the exception: for six of the seven models, between 13% and 31% of the generated contracts tha

papers.title: Revisiting Cauchy-Schwarz Norm Bounds for SDC Detection in LLM Inference
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) execute billions of floating-point operations per output token across many hardware accelerators. At this scale, hardware-induced faults can bypass system-level detection mechanisms and cause Silent Data Corruption (SDC). Algorithm-Based Fault Tolerance (ABFT) is the state-of-the-art technique for protecting matrix multiplication from such faults, but it incurs non-negligible computational overhead and requires thresholds to distinguish hardware-induced errors from floating-point roundoff. In this paper, we revisit Cauchy--Schwarz Norm Bounds (CSNB) as a low-overhead alternative for detecting SDC during LLM inference. We compare CSNB against ABFT through controlled fault injection and evaluate the runtime overhead of both verification and threshold determination across multiple model sizes, batch sizes, and generation lengths. Our results show that, on average, CSNB retains 99% of the fault detection capability of ABFT for the evaluated linear layers in dense LLMs, while reducing verification overhead by 87% and threshold determination overhead by 67%. For Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) router gate computations, however, CSNB retains only 55% of the fault detection capability of ABFT. These findings suggest that CSNB is a promising low-overhead alternative for protecting linear layers in dense LLMs, while checksum-based verification remains preferable for the evaluated MoE router gate.

papers.title: From Observations to Authorized Actions: Measuring Source Information in Android Agents
papers.abstract: Android agents read content from applications and web pages and act on it with the user's authority, yet they cannot reliably tell where that content came from -- its source, the application or document that supplied it. The WebView accessibility fields we inspected expose the host application but omit the document origins available inside the browser, so an agent reading through this interface cannot check which document supplied an object; a limited reproduction on an unmodified WebView yields the same finding. We build and separately evaluate two prototypes to examine how source information supports authorization. Our application-source monitor withholds side-effecting calls whose signed source record contains an untrusted application. With the source set derived from the OS accessibility log, it blocked every selected attack write in the tested runs, but it also withheld benign sends issued after reading untrusted content, flagged benign tasks that use external content, and carried source records into a later clean task. Our WebView source-reference gate uses records from a modified browser to check object origins and reference lifetime through direct calls; in a separate 24-trial evaluation, the live agent selected no disallowed object. Supporting benchmark and planner measurements characterize textual argument matches and attacker-target selection, without establishing causal dataflow or a controlled model ranking. The prototypes are not an integrated defense: the WebVi

papers.title: TenonAgent: Virtualizing Execution Residency for Memory-Oversubscribed LLM Agents
papers.abstract: LLM agents execute as long-lived, multi-stage workflows with substantial resource-demand variation across phases. Provisioning each agent or sandbox for its lifetime peak leads to low resource utilization, particularly for memory, whereas aggressive oversubscription risks memory contention, out-of-memory failures, and costly workflow retries. This tension limits the concurrency and efficiency of agent serving under constrained host memory. We present TenonAgent, a runtime system that virtualizes sandbox residency by decoupling the logical agent's lifetime from its physical execution environment. To manage memory oversubscription, TenonAgent employs a dual-timescale control plane. At action boundaries, it combines predictive admission control with a fail-closed, restart-safe contract, dynamically materializing or dematerializing sandboxes based on global memory pressure. During active tool execution, a sched_ext-based kernel gate paces sandbox execution permissions to reduce unexpected concurrent memory growth. The gate provides feedback control over future execution opportunities. Evaluations across diverse agentic workloads show that, under the tested workloads and parameter settings, TenonAgent substantially reduces observed OOM failures and achieves a 100% task success rate in bursts reaching an 8.6x memory oversubscription ratio. Overall, it delivers up to a 5.5x speedup over unmanaged execution, outperforms existing agent-level and cgroup-based schedulers by 5x to 37x, a

papers.title: GMM: Generalized OS Memory Management for Programmable XPUs
papers.abstract: Since the AI boom, the fast evolving programmable XPU devices utilize high-bandwidth local memory to accelerate domain-specific tasks offloaded from the host CPU, resulting in a proliferation of XPU memory management systems implemented in proprietary drivers. However, existing OS core memory management (MM) continues to lack a high-level software abstraction, excluding the XPUs from leveraging OS advanced memory features. The XPU manufacturers have to reimplement independent XPU MM drivers, exacerbating the fragmented XPU software ecosystem. This paper presents GMM, generalized memory management that provides unified MM subsystems for XPUs. By adding an explicit logical mapping abstraction, GMM 1) provides universal NUMA-aware memory API for XPUs; 2) allows ease of XPU MM delegation; 3) enables sharing of advanced XPU memory features. Lightweight XPU MM drivers are implemented for two representative XPU manufacturers, Nvidia and Huawei. Both GMM-based drivers obtain competitive performance compared with their vendor-supplied drivers. GMM also obtains up to 41% higher fault-driven page migration throughput. Two real-world industrial case studies are exercised, where GMM reduces XPU memory utilization by 10% with up to 22.6x faster inference serving switch latency.

papers.title: Scoring Explanations Without Reading Them: Structural Shortcuts in Automated-Interpretability Evaluation Data
papers.abstract: Automated interpretability scores an explanation of a sparse-autoencoder (SAE) feature by asking a model to predict, token by token, where the feature fires on evaluation examples or to judge whether marked tokens fit it. We find that the evaluation data standard pipelines build can be scored without reading the explanation. On Neuronpedia's stored fuzzing runs for 500 random GPT-2 small features, 91.3% of activating examples are cropped with the peak on the centre token, and a rule that says "yes" when the centre token is marked reaches balanced accuracy 0.979, against 0.838 for the stored LLM scorers (recomputed from the stored per-item verdicts, on marks rebuilt from the pipeline's code); a rule reading only the mark count reaches 0.969. The cue changes form across pipelines: current delphi always marks the same slot in its fuzzing negatives, and full-context runs mark negatives with more tokens. OpenAI's simulation benchmark lists each neuron's top-activating sequences first; a rule that predicts activity on the first five scores 0.227 in pooled correlation against 0.160 for GPT-4's published simulator (post hoc). We give closed forms for what such rules can score; show that one scorer's simulation scores are higher on stored snippets than on natural windows but not shown to be reordered; and build windows that remove the position cue, derive but do not build negatives that remove the mark cues, and separate the sequence cue by decomposition. On natural-text windows cut a

papers.title: GPU-resident Execution for Timing-predictable Sensor Processing Systems
papers.abstract: Real-time embedded systems increasingly place GPU-accelerated processing of high-bandwidth sensor streams inside closed-loop systems, but the CPU (the host) remains the primary orchestrator of each iteration. The host observes sensor inputs, submits CUDA work, waits for completion, and commits actuation. This host-mediated path exposes the closed-loop end-to-end latency to I/O interrupts, host scheduler decisions, and CUDA API overheads even after common host-side mitigations such as GPU-memory RDMA or CPU core isolation. This paper presents GPU-resident Execution, a new execution model for real-time sensor processing pipelines that keeps I/O and GPU execution in a long-lived device-resident loop. Sensor inputs arrive in GPU memory, trigger GPU-side processing, and reach GPU-visible output endpoints without any host wakeups. We implement the model in the NVIDIA Holoscan C++ framework and provide reference components for building GPU-resident applications. We evaluate our system on NVIDIA GPUs and SoCs with inference, host-contention, multi-loop, and streaming camera workloads. On an industry-grade 1080p, 60 Hz real-time camera-to-display application, GPU-resident Execution reduces photon-to-display jitter from 4.83 ms to 0.66 ms (7.3x) relative to a CPU-driven GPU-memory RDMA baseline and reduces software-processing jitter from 1.70 ms to 0.01 ms (170x).

papers.title: Ember: Making Unified Virtual Memory Practical for Discrete-Memory GPUs
papers.abstract: GPU working sets have outgrown GPU memory, so applications must oversubscribe it, keeping only hot data on the GPU. NVIDIA's Unified Virtual Memory (UVM) supports oversubscription, but its performance degrades once data exceeds the GPU's memory. This stems from its fault-driven data placement, wasting interconnect bandwidth, and underutilizing the GPU. This raises the question: can UVM oversubscription become practical on stock GPUs, exploiting GPU memory speed and minimizing wasted interconnect bandwidth, without placement hints, profiling runs, or application changes? To this end, we present Ember, a UVM management framework for oversubscribed workloads. Ember introduces a hybrid address space; allocations start as mapped into host memory, omitting data migration. Ember's counter-driven region promotion uses GPU's hardware counters to fetch hot regions to the GPU, its decay-based eager reclamation proactively evicts cold regions in batches, while via online region re-placement, Ember tracks the hot set at runtime. We implement Ember within NVIDIA's open-source UVM driver for unmodified applications and as a userspace variant on stock CUDA. At 1.5x oversubscription, it is 6.8-10.6x faster than UVM on six applications across three PCIe GPUs, and generates LLM tokens 4.7-16x faster at sizes where manual placement cannot run at all. Without a profiling run, it beats a profile-guided alternative by 2.1x on kernel time.

papers.title: Characterizing CPU-GPU Memory Sharing over Unified Memory Architecture
papers.abstract: Unified Memory Architecture (UMA) enables the CPU and GPU to share a single physical memory. However, its complexity and opacity often drive applications back to inefficient copying or to incorrect direct access that sacrifices performance or even correctness. This paper presents a comprehensive study of CPU-GPU memory sharing on UMA, covering correctness and performance across data-plane transmission and control-plane coordination on four platforms. It yields four findings that guide libumsh, a portable library that delivers correct and efficient memory sharing across platforms and extends to emerging ones (e.g., NVIDIA DGX Spark). Applied to nine real-world systems, libumsh reduces data-plane time by 16-75% and control-plane overhead by 7-90%.

papers.title: PredictIO: Decoupling Workload Prediction from OS-Controlled Storage Prefetching
papers.abstract: Storage stalls remain a significant source of application latency even on fast storage devices. Prefetching can hide part of this latency by fetching data before it is demanded, but general-purpose operating-system mechanisms typically infer future accesses from recent file offsets. This approach is ineffective when accesses are determined by workload structure, such as recurring sparse accesses during application launch, logical traversal in database scans, or model-layout metadata in LLM runtimes. Existing workload-aware prefetchers usually embed prediction logic inside individual applications and couple execution to application-level I/O paths, making policies difficult to reuse across workloads and systems. We present PredictIO, a programmable interface that separates workload prediction from prefetch execution. PredictIO delivers kernel-observed accesses and application hints to user-space policies, which express predictions as uniform page-range requests. A kernel-space executor validates, bounds, and filters these requests against cached and in-flight pages before issuing asynchronous prefetch I/O. We implement PredictIO for application launch, SQLite range scans, and LLM model loading. Across these workloads, PredictIO reduces latency by 5.3-26.3%, achieves up to 2.99x speedup for SQLite scans, and reduces LLM loading latency by 8.8-47.9%. We further show that a common prediction policy can be reused across SQLite and LMDB through lightweight adapters, that an applica

papers.title: ToFu: Exploiting and Fuzzing the LLM-Orchestrator-Tool Trust Boundary
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as agents that interact with external software through tools, with an orchestration layer translating model outputs into structured tool invocations. This architecture creates an LLM-orchestrator-tool trust boundary where tool semantics may go unenforced and LLM-generated arguments may be incorrectly treated as trusted. We present ToFu, a tool-aware framework that automatically derives semantic security checks for LLM tools from their existing metadata and a CWE-guided sanitizer corpus. ToFu specializes these checks to individual tools and automatically generates fuzzing harnesses and semantic oracles using runtime introspection and outcome sanitization. We evaluated ToFu across 273 MCP servers containing 3405 tools and identified verified bugs corresponding to CWE weakness classes in 343 tools across 118 of the servers. Our findings show that real-world tools frequently fail to enforce their documented input semantics, making it unsafe to treat LLM-generated arguments as trusted.

papers.title: Enabling Extended SGX Enclaves inside Confidential Virtual Machines
papers.abstract: Confidential Virtual Machines (CVMs), such as AMD SEV-SNP, and process enclaves, such as Intel SGX, provide workload protection against cloud threats. However, they strongly differ in TCB, deployment cost and speed, peer workload protection, resource sharing, fine-grained isolation and attestation, and programming capabilities. Nesting process enclaves within CVMs offers an optimal solution and an opportunity to address long-standing SGX limitations: lack of intra-enclave protection, expensive transitions and exception paths, slow enclave cloning, and a restricted programming model that limits Library Operating Systems (LibOS). This paper introduces TEEVisor, a CVM-resident architecture consisting of a security monitor and a kernel driver that leverages AMD SEV-SNP Virtual Machine Privilege Levels (VMPLs) to build hardware-protected, process-level enclaves inside a guest CVM with two modes: (1) an SGX binary compatibility mode to run unmodified SGX applications; and (2) a novel extended SGX~(eSGX) mode optimizing slow execution paths and offering richer enclave programming capabilities. On commercial AMD EPYC hardware, against native CVM execution, TEEVisor incurs under 5% overhead on compute- and memory-bound workloads, around 12% on I/O-heavy applications, and accelerates enclave cloning to a rate of 93~$μ$s/MB of enclave size, demonstrating that eSGX semantics inside a CVM are practical for production use.

papers.title: Mole: Tier-Specific Hotness Profiling Driven Memory Tiering for Multi-Tiered Memory Systems
papers.abstract: Multi-tiered memory systems combine fast, small upper tiers with slow, large lower tiers to improve performance and cost efficiency. Existing designs, such as AutoTiering and MTM, rely on greedy promotion and stepwise demotion, which can intensify contention for limited capacity in faster tiers. We observe that promotions directly improve performance, whereas demotions primarily reclaim space. Based on this asymmetry, we propose Mole, a memory tiering system that separates promotion and demotion destinations. Mole employs staging demotion to move cold pages directly to the lowest tier, bypassing intermediate tiers, and targeted promotion to place hot pages in tiers that match their current hotness. The lowest tier serves as a staging area from which pages can be promoted when they become hot again. This separation preserves intermediate-tier capacity for promotions, reducing tier contention and migration failures. However, staging demotion requires timely identification of pages that become hot after demotion. To meet this requirement with low profiling overhead, Mole uses tier-specific profiling: it profiles the lowest tier at high frequency to detect reactivated hot pages, while profiling upper tiers at lower frequency to identify cold pages. Experimental results show that Mole reduces migration failures and improves performance under dynamic access patterns.

papers.title: Behind a Simple Read: Understanding Work and Waiting in the Linux I/O Stack
papers.abstract: A simple read interface provides uniform semantics but unpredictable performance. Using synchronous large-buffer Linux reads, we decompose the buffered-read path into work volume, processing time, and critical-path exposure. Reducing local cost or accelerating request submission need not shorten a complete read. Linux uses large folios to reduce metadata work and I/O-copy overlap to hide most cold-read copying; an experimental kernel prototype shows that more aggressive overlap and parallelism can shorten the host path when these mechanisms fail. Device waiting dominates SSD cold reads. We abstract first-completion wait F and subsequent completion capacity B_CQ from request-batch timelines. Real-SSD experiments characterize their variation with request and batch size, while MQSim traces explain their internal origins. A wait chain along the folio-bio-request mapping connects device completion to upper-layer waiting. Under strict batching, the median absolute cross-layer prediction error is at most 7.43%. Finally, we apply the completion model and wait chain to request supply, Linux readahead, data layout, and waiting policies. Cases cover gains, no gains, and reversals, comparing predictions with interventions to close the loop from observation and modeling to understanding and control and provide a measurable basis for layered I/O decisions.

papers.title: Training Parallel Speculative Draft Models by Directly Minimizing Expected Decoding Rounds
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference by using a low-cost draft model to propose tokens that the full-size target model verifies in parallel. Parallel and semi-autoregressive (semi- AR) drafters improve drafting efficiency by proposing an entire block in a single forward pass, but training them raises a new difficulty: the draft distribution for a given position depends on where the decoding round starts, and where rounds start depends on how many tokens earlier rounds accepted. Existing training objectives typically rely on block-local surrogates that ignore this cross-round coupling, and therefore do not directly optimize the global decoding efficiency. In this work, we develop a theoretical framework for training and evaluating these drafters by representing speculative decoding as a Markov reward process. This formulation yields the Expected Decoding Rounds (EDR) objective, which weights local rejection costs by state occupancies and exactly equals the expected number of decoding rounds. Unlike prior surrogate objectives, EDR introduces no auxiliary hyperparameters. We then derive an exact temporal-difference gradient that supports unbiased stochastic optimization from target-model rollouts. The same framework also yields an exact offline evaluator for round counts, enabling paired drafter comparisons on shared target rollouts without running speculative decoding. Finetuning two state-of-the- art drafters, DSpark and DFly, with EDR consistently i

papers.title: Trail: Scalable and Low-Cost Temporal TLB Prefetching via Page-Table-Embedded Deltas
papers.abstract: Address translation is a major bottleneck in data-intensive workloads. TLB prefetching can hide translation latency, but existing spatial prefetchers struggle with irregular accesses, while temporal prefetchers store address deltas in fixed-capacity hardware that cannot scale with application memory footprints. Our characterization of 200 translation-intensive workloads reveals that each virtual memory region has a small, recurring set of deltas, and over 94% of deltas fit in 18 signed bits. We introduce Trail, a temporal TLB prefetcher that stores deltas in unused bits of leaf page table entries (PTEs). When a region triggers a page table walk, Trail identifies the region that last triggered a walk from the same instruction and records their delta in that source region's PTE. When a later walk fetches the source region's PTE cache block, Trail retrieves its deltas without additional memory accesses and prefetches translations for likely destination regions into the TLBs and cache hierarchy. Storing multiple deltas per PTE cache block improves coverage, while using existing PTE bits allows metadata capacity to scale with the application's memory footprint without additional metadata storage. Across 200 workloads and 100 multiprogrammed mixes, Trail improves single-core (four-core) performance by 5.7% (11.5%) on average over a baseline without TLB prefetching, outperforming the best prior standalone TLB prefetcher by 1.7% (2.5%). Trail requires only a 64-entry hardware table t

papers.title: TopoCurve: Geometry-Aware Topology Reasoning via Bézier Curves in Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract: Topology reasoning jointly detects 3D lanes and traffic elements from multi-view images and infers their structural connectivity. Current methods model lanes as discrete polylines, lacking smoothness, analytical tangent directions, and global spatial support for attention, while providing sparse topology supervision. We propose TopoCurve, a geometry-driven architecture for 3D topology reasoning grounded in a structured parametric lane representation. Lanes are modeled as endpoint-fixed cubic Bézier curves, enabling continuous geometry with exact endpoints and analytically defined directionality. We exploit this shared curve geometry across the entire pipeline. Endpoint distance and tangent alignment are encoded with multi-scale Fourier features and injected into the topology head. Sampled curve points serve as geometry-aligned references for deformable cross-attention spanning the full lane. Parallel curve-anchored attention branches provide diverse predictions for one-to-many topology supervision. These components form a tightly coupled cascade where representation enables geometric reasoning, guides feature aggregation, and supports denser supervision. TopoCurve achieves 50.6 OLS on the OpenLane-V2 benchmark without any post-processing, establishing a new state-of-the-art among end-to-end camera-only methods, and outperforms all existing approaches on endpoint detection (56.8 vs. 52.6 on DET_p).

papers.title: WarpDRF: The Unwritten Contract of GPU Warp Programming
papers.abstract: Warp primitives such as tensor core operations, shuffles, reductions, and barriers are critical to high-performance GPU kernels, and every major GPU language supports some set of them. The threads that participate in a primitive, and therefore synchronize, are determined dynamically by how threads diverge and reconverge, and by intra-warp scheduling such as independent thread scheduling. In practice, many high-performance kernels use these primitives and behave as expected, following an intuitive but unwritten data-race-freedom contract that has never been stated precisely or empirically tested. We present WarpDRF, the first abstract warp programming model to make this contract precise, with participation rules parameterized by reconvergence guarantees and per-primitive requirements so that instantiations match different GPU languages. We prove (formalized in Rocq) that a kernel satisfying WarpDRF executes every warp primitive with the participants the reference semantics assigns and produces the same results, so a programmer can reason in the reference semantics alone. We implement the model in MLIR with a reference interpreter and fuzz 10K conformance tests for each of three configurations across CUDA, HIP, HLSL, Metal, and SPIR-V on 16 device and backend pairs; at least one WarpDRF configuration describes each, with CUDA honoring the strictly weakest configuration. Finally, we extend Faial, a static data-race analyzer for CUDA, into the first DRF checker for an empirically

papers.title: PRA-TLS: Attestation of a Client Application for TEE
papers.abstract: Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) are secure foundations for protecting sensitive information and executing computations over confidential data. Processing in an isolated execution environment (enclave) is invoked by an untrusted application in the Rich Execution Environment (REE). Then the enclave returns the execution results to the untrusted application. Even if the enclave has been attested, the boundary between the enclave and the untrusted application poses risks, such as tampering with input arguments or return values and manipulating the order in which the application invokes functions. Therefore, it is necessary to establish the authenticity and integrity of not only the enclave itself but also the application and its execution environment. In this study, we propose an attestation protocol, Portable Remote Attestation TLS (PRA-TLS), for a client application that invokes an enclave. We introduce a daemon that acts as an attester. PRA-TLS uses a trusted Attester Daemon to measure the state of the host environment and application code at runtime, providing these measurements as attestation evidence for verification by a remote Verifier. This mechanism allows the enclave to proceed only when the software environment is in the expected state and the application code is verified as legitimate. We define attack models and security requirements for the proposed protocol and formally evaluate its security using the Tamarin Prover. Furthermore, we implement a prototype of

papers.title: No More Translation at Runtime: LLM-Empowered Static Binary Translation
papers.abstract: While AArch64 CPUs are becoming strong market contenders, their software ecosystem lags behind the mature x86-64 environment, hindering the adoption of the new architectures and impacting user experience. Binary translation bridges this divide by converting binary code from one architecture (e.g., x86-64) to run on another (e.g., AArch64), allowing legacy software to benefit from modern hardware's performance and energy efficiency advantages. Current translation methods are typically either dynamic, which adds significant runtime overhead, or static, which struggles with reliability due to the inherent complexities of binary analysis. This paper introduces a new static, assembly-to-assembly translation paradigm that transforms binary code ahead of execution, generating portable, efficient native-like binaries that run on AArch64 devices without runtime frameworks. Benefiting from recent breakthroughs in large language models (LLMs), we provide a practical and automated translation engine that produces high-quality code with minimal human intervention. To ensure correctness, we introduce a crucial verification step, where we split the assembly code into simplified snippets, enabling efficient and scalable semantic verification. Our evaluation shows that this approach significantly outperforms existing open-source solutions with a large margin, producing binaries with near-native performance. Furthermore, it shows substantial improvements over the leading industrial translator,

papers.title: Deep Defence on Wheels: A Dual Intrusion Detection System Architecture for Comprehensive In-Vehicle Network Security
papers.abstract: Increasing connectivity to the outside world and the lack of inbuilt security mechanisms have made legacy intra-vehicular networks vulnerable to cyberattacks. Initial research focused on maximising detection accuracy for known and unknown attacks, often using large, full-precision machine learning models. However, embedding IDSs into vehicular electronic systems also requires low detection latency, energy efficiency and minimal electronic control unit (ECU) resource overhead to process about 2,000 CAN frames/s. Lightweight models must balance accuracy with these deployment constraints. We propose a dual IDS framework comprising supervised and unsupervised learning-based solutions, each optimised for real-time, resource-constrained automotive platforms. A quantised LSTM-based IDS (QLSTM-IDS) achieves over 99.9% detection accuracy for DoS/Flooding, Fuzzing and Spoofing/Malfunction attacks using a single model architecture evaluated on two widely used datasets. The model is trained using the Brevitas quantisation-aware training library, transformed into a dataflow accelerator with custom blocks compatible with AMD's FINN toolchain, and synthesised using Vitis HLS. Complementing this, an 8-bit quantised convolutional autoencoder-based IDS (QCAE-IDS), quantised using AMD's Vitis-AI toolchain, detects previously unseen anomalies that alter CAN-ID sequence patterns with over 99% accuracy. An integration architecture enables both models to operate on a single FPGA, bridging the netwo

papers.title: RetainZ: Reclaim-Time-Aware Placement for AI Checkpoints on Zoned SSDs
papers.abstract: Solid State Drives (SSDs) are becoming the dominant medium for performance-critical storage. Zoned Namespace (ZNS) SSDs are getting more and more attractive because sequential writes and explicit zone resets reduce address-mapping, over-provisioning, and internal garbage-collection costs. However, reclaiming space requires resetting an entire zone, so deleting one file does not free its space while other files there must be kept. This erase-before-write constraint becomes a bottleneck for write-intensive workloads, particularly AI checkpointing during model training, where frequent saves of model and optimizer state compete for space with long-retained checkpoints. We observe that retention policies inherently encode when data can be retired, avoiding the need for a learned lifetime predictor. We present RetainZ, a storage backend that translates these policies into explicit reclaim epochs. Its allocator isolates long-retained data and groups objects with nearby reclaim epochs, balancing delayed space reclamation against unused space at zone ends. Evaluated on FEMU with multi-tenant streams and checkpoint manifests up to Pythia-1B, RetainZ reduces space occupied by deleted data and unused zone tails by 41.7% and mean per-input checkpoint p99 latency by 47.5% at 84% target load compared with the allocator of ZenFS, an established lifetime-aware ZNS backend, and lowers host write amplification from 1.165 to 1.003.

papers.title: Optimal Dynamic Resource Allocation for Multicore Real-time Systems
papers.abstract: We formulate a novel optimal control problem for data-driven dynamic resource allocation in multicore real-time systems. The proposed formulation accounts for hard deadline constraints and resource bounds. Under mild assumptions, we prove several results on the feasibility and existence of optimal solution for the proposed formulation. Building on these analyses, we design an algorithm to solve the multi-core dynamic resource allocation problem. We demonstrate the practical use of this new algorithm by experimentally evaluating it on a real multicore platform using four benchmarks from the literature.

papers.title: When Agent Context Goes Stale: Incoherence in Volatile Agent Context
papers.abstract: Modern agents increasingly ground their reasoning in observations returned by tools, such as file contents read from a workspace. However, the data sources underlying these observations may later be modified by users, other agents, or external tools, while the model retains only the stale content in its context window. Existing agent runtimes provide little support for notifying the model that a previously observed fact has become stale, causing agents to reuse outdated observations and make incorrect claims about the current workspace state. We propose Concord, a context coherence framework that maintains the consistency between tool observation in agent context and the mutable sources from which they were derived. Concord links each observation to its source, detects source changes, and uses configurable handling policies to update, annotate, or suppress stale context before reuse. Concord is applicable across different agent runtimes and external resources, and can be easily extended to new runtime-resource settings. We implement Concord as a general framework, and instantiate a concrete use case to assess its effectiveness. We construct ConcordBench, where previously observed file contents become stale after subsequent edits. Across three evaluated frontier models, Concord produces answers consistent with the restored workspace state in all evaluated cases under these constructed conditions, matching the oracle on recover count for this benchmark, while using 46.4% fewer

papers.title: Awkernel: RTOS Bridging DAG Scheduling Theory and Component-Oriented Real-Time Systems Practice
papers.abstract: Real-time directed acyclic graph (DAG) scheduling provides a rigorous basis for timing analysis and efficiency in component-oriented real-time systems (CORTS) such as autonomous driving systems, yet challenges remain from the perspectives of both theorists and practitioners. For theorists, no OS natively supports the DAG task model; algorithms are therefore evaluated only analytically or in simulation, ignoring real-hardware overheads. For practitioners, today's CORTS platforms (ROS~2 and AUTOSAR Adaptive Platform) are designed for service composition rather than timing analyzability; adopting DAG scheduling research therefore demands substantial code changes and developer discipline. This paper proposes Awkernel, the first open-source real-time operating system (RTOS) that natively supports real-time DAG scheduling research, bridging DAG scheduling theory and CORTS practice. For theorists, Awkernel is a real-hardware testbed: it exposes a modular OS-native DAG scheduler for easy algorithm implementation, plus a random workload generator and built-in metrics for evaluation. For practitioners, Awkernel is not a full replacement for today's platforms but a CORTS platform maximizing timing analyzability: its familiar publish/subscribe model keeps porting mechanical, mapping each callback to one subtask. Moreover, its function-as-subtask (FasS) API enforces DAG semantics (precedence constraints) without programmer discipline, yielding applications that match the theoretical DAG m

papers.title: LLM-Based Test Generation: Information Sources, Generation Strategies, and Quality Evidence
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to generate test scenarios, executable test suites, assertions, interaction sequences, and fuzzing infrastructure. These artifacts serve different purposes and rely on different sources of information about correct behavior. A test that increases implementation coverage, a test that agrees with a reference program, and a test that detects a requirements violation therefore provide distinct kinds of evidence. We present a structured narrative survey that connects the generation process to the evidence used to justify test quality. Drawing on 95 curated source records through 29 September 2026, we organize the field along four dimensions: testing objectives and artifacts, information available during training and generation, generation and learning mechanisms, and evaluation evidence. We synthesize work on unit and requirements-based testing, test oracles, API and GUI testing, fuzzing, and learned test generators. The resulting framework explains how execution feedback can improve executability while also affecting the independence of an oracle, why specification provenance and training-time reference supervision matter for comparisons, and how downstream code-selection gains differ from test correctness. We use these distinctions to organize benchmarks and derive a research agenda for independent oracle assessment, budget-aware generation, repository-scale evaluation, and test maintenance.

papers.title: Pattern-Guided Graph Synthesis for Suppressing Known Defects in DL Compiler Fuzzing
papers.abstract: Fuzzing is effective at finding bugs in deep learning (DL) compilers, but existing fuzzers repeatedly trigger faults they have already uncovered. Current fuzzers diversify the generated programs, and downstream tools deduplicate bug reports post hoc, but neither stops a fuzzer from generating programs that re-trigger known defects. We present Reprise, a DL compiler fuzzer that suppresses reports of known defects during test generation.
